title: Exam FM — Financial Mathematics
subtitle: Make the time value of money intuitive, then automatic. Every cash flow becomes a picture you can price on sight.
intro: FM is one idea stretched across five modules: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow, and everything — annuities, loans, bonds, immunization — is just that idea applied to a particular pattern of cash flows. We teach the timeline picture first, the formula second, and the calculator shortcut third. Each concept ends in a timed, BA II-style mastery gate; miss it and spaced repetition brings it back until pricing a cash flow is as natural as reading a clock.

format.passing: Grade 6 or higher on the SOA 0–10 scale — about 70% correct. 35 questions in 3.5 hours is 6 minutes each; a financial calculator (BA II Plus or equivalent) is allowed and essential.

modules.title: Time Value of Money
modules.blurb: The bedrock. Accumulation and discounting, effective vs nominal rates, the force of interest, and equations of value. Small on the syllabus, foundational for everything after.

concepts.title: Interest & Accumulation
concepts.tagline: A dollar today grows; a future dollar shrinks back to today. Compound interest is the engine, and it runs faster than your intuition expects.

sections.body: Here is the one sentence the whole exam rests on: **a dollar is only meaningful once you say *when* it is paid.** Money at different dates lives in different worlds, and you cannot add, compare, or equate amounts until you drag them all onto the *same* date. Accumulating pushes a dollar forward in time; discounting pulls a future dollar back to today. Every annuity, loan, bond, and immunization problem you will ever see is this single move, repeated. Spend real effort here and the rest of FM stops being a list of formulas and becomes one idea wearing different costumes.

sections.title: Why money grows at all — and why it grows as a curve
sections.body:
Lending a dollar means giving up the chance to use it. Interest is the rent the borrower pays for that year of use. So far that explains a straight line: charge the same rent every year and you get **simple interest**. But real money does something sneakier. After one year your dollar has *become* $1+i$ dollars — and that whole amount, interest included, can now be lent out. The next year's rent is charged on the larger pile. Interest starts earning interest. That feedback loop is **compound interest**, and feedback loops do not grow in straight lines — they curve upward, faster and faster.

Hold that picture: simple interest is a *line* because the principal never changes; compound interest is a *curve* because the principal quietly grows under you every year. Over one year they are identical. Over a career they are not even close — and every actuarial cash flow assumes the compound curve, because that is how invested money actually behaves.

sections.title: Building the accumulation formula one year at a time
sections.body:
Do not memorize $(1+i)^t$ — *watch it assemble itself.* Start with \$1 and an effective annual rate $i$ (effective means: the actual fraction your money grows in one year, no fine print).

After **year 1** you have your dollar plus its rent: $1 + i = (1+i)$.

After **year 2** that entire amount earns another year's rent. You do not add $i$ again — you *scale* the whole pile by $(1+i)$: $$(1+i)\times(1+i) = (1+i)^2.$$

After **year 3**, scale again: $(1+i)^2\times(1+i) = (1+i)^3$. The pattern is now undeniable — each year multiplies by one more factor of $(1+i)$ — so after $t$ years: $$A(t) = A(0)\,(1+i)^t.$$

The exponent counts *how many times the pile got rescaled*. That is the entire content of compound interest. Compare it with simple interest, where only the original principal earns: $A(t) = A(0)(1 + it)$ — addition, not multiplication, which is exactly why it stays a line.

sections.title: Discounting is just accumulation run backwards
sections.body:
If multiplying by $(1+i)$ moves a dollar *forward* one year, then **dividing** by $(1+i)$ must move it *backward* one year — undoing the growth. The present value of \$1 due in one year is therefore $$v = \frac{1}{1+i},$$ the **discount factor** — the single most reused number on the exam. It answers: *what is one future dollar worth to me right now?* Less than a dollar, because I lose a year of growth.

Pull a payment back $t$ years by dividing $t$ times, i.e. multiplying by $v^t$: $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1+i)^t} = FV\cdot v^t.$$

Accumulating and discounting are perfect inverses: $(1+i)^t$ and $v^t$ are reciprocals, so pushing a dollar forward five years and then back five years lands you exactly where you started. Once you *feel* that $v$ is just 'one step backward in time,' present-value algebra stops being a formula to recall and becomes a direction to walk.

sections.title: See the line and the curve pull apart

widget.caption: Start \$1000. First set the rate low (2%) and short (3 years) — simple and compound nearly overlap, which is why people underrate compounding. Now push the rate to 8% and the horizon to 30 years and watch the compound curve tear away from the simple line. The growing gap *is* interest-on-interest made visible. The continuous curve (force of interest) is the same idea taken to its smooth limit — the ceiling compounding approaches as you compound ever more often.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — move one payment both directions
sections.body: At an effective annual rate of 6%, find (a) the value at time 5 of \$1000 paid today, and (b) the value today of \$1000 paid at time 5. Doing both on one number shows accumulation and discounting are mirror images.
steps: **Set up the direction.** Part (a) moves money *forward* 5 years → multiply by $(1+i)^5$. Part (b) moves money *backward* 5 years → multiply by $v^5$.

**Sanity check the mirror:** $1338.23 \times 0.74726 \approx 1000$ and $747.26 \times 1.33823 \approx 1000$. Forward then backward returns the original dollar — the two factors are reciprocals, exactly as the theory promised.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — solve for the unknown rate
sections.body: Exam questions rarely hand you $i$. More often you know where money started and ended and must *back out* the rate. An investment of \$2000 grows to \$2800 in 4 years under compound interest. Find the effective annual rate $i$.
steps: **Write the accumulation equation:** $2000(1+i)^4 = 2800$.
**Isolate the growth factor:** $(1+i)^4 = 2800/2000 = 1.4$.
**Undo the exponent with a root** (the inverse of raising to the 4th power): $1+i = 1.4^{1/4} = 1.4^{0.25}$.
**Read off the rate:** $i = 0.08776 \approx 8.78\%$. Always solving for a rate follows this same arc: isolate $(1+i)^t$, then take the $t$-th root.

sections.title: The Rule of 72 — and the proof that makes it trustworthy
sections.body:
The shortcut: **money doubles in roughly $72/(100i)$ years.** At 6% that is $72/6 = 12$ years; at 8%, $72/8 = 9$ years. But a shortcut you cannot derive is a shortcut you cannot trust at the edges — so here is exactly where the 72 comes from.

**Derivation.** Doubling means $(1+i)^t = 2$. Take natural logs of both sides: $t\,\ln(1+i) = \ln 2$, so $$t = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+i)} = \frac{0.693}{\ln(1+i)}.$$ For the small rates on the exam, $\ln(1+i)\approx i$ (e.g. $\ln 1.08 = 0.0770$ vs $i = 0.08$). Substituting gives $t \approx 0.693/i = 69.3/(100i)$ — the **Rule of 69.3**, which is *exactly* right for continuous compounding.

**So why 72, not 69.3?** Two reasons stacked. First, $\ln(1+i)$ is slightly *smaller* than $i$, which makes the true doubling time slightly *longer* than $69.3/(100i)$ predicts — bumping the numerator up corrects for it. Second, 72 is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12 — clean mental arithmetic. The 72 is a deliberate fudge that happens to be most accurate right in the 6%–10% band the exam loves. Use it to *gut-check*, never to answer: if your computed accumulation implies a doubling time wildly off the Rule-of-72 estimate, you mis-keyed a rate or an exponent.

sections.title: The rate and the exponent must speak the same time unit
sections.body: This is the single most common TVM mistake, and it is always the same shape: the rate is quoted *per year* but the clock is ticking in *months* (or vice versa). You cannot write $(1+0.06)^{24}$ for 24 months at 6% annual — that compounds 6% **twenty-four times**, a wildly wrong answer. Two legal fixes: (1) keep time in years, $(1.06)^{2}$ for 24 months; or (2) convert the rate to a monthly effective rate $1.06^{1/12}-1$ first, *then* use the exponent 24. Whichever you pick, **one** conversion, and the rate's period and the exponent's period must match before you press a key. When a problem mixes annual rates with monthly cash flows, stop and pick a single time unit on purpose before touching the calculator.

cards.front: Why is compound growth a curve while simple growth is a line?
cards.back: Compound interest charges next year's interest on the *grown* balance (multiply by $(1+i)$ each year → exponential curve); simple interest only ever pays on the fixed original principal (add $i$ each year → straight line).

cards.front: What does the discount factor $v=1/(1+i)$ actually *mean*?
cards.back: The value today of \$1 paid one year from now — one step backward in time. Discounting is accumulation run in reverse, so $v^t$ and $(1+i)^t$ are reciprocals.

questions.q: At an effective annual rate of 5%, what is the accumulated value of \$2000 after 3 years?
What is the present value of \$5000 due in 4 years at 7% effective annual interest?
An account earns simple interest of 8% per year. How much does \$1000 grow to in 5 years?
How long until money doubles at 9% effective annual interest (use exact compound interest)?
questions.explain: $(1.09)^t = 2 \Rightarrow t = \ln 2/\ln 1.09 = 0.6931/0.08618 \approx 8.04$ years. (Rule of 72 gives ~8.)

questions.q: \$800 today and \$X in 2 years are together worth \$2000 today at 10% effective. Find $X$.
An account earns 6% annual effective interest. To the nearest year, how long until a single deposit triples in value?
questions.explain: Solve $(1.06)^n = 3$: $n = \frac{\ln 3}{\ln 1.06} = \frac{1.0986}{0.0583} = 18.85$, rounding to 19 years. The 'Rule of 72' style shortcut $72/6 = 12$ estimates *doubling*, not tripling — that is the trap answer.

questions.q: 1000 is invested for 3 years at 8% annual effective, then the balance is reinvested for 2 more years at 5% annual effective. Calculate the accumulated value at the end of year 5.
questions.explain: Accumulate through each rate in turn: $1000(1.08)^3(1.05)^2 = 1000(1.259712)(1.1025) = 1388.83$. Using 8% for all 5 years gives 1469.33; using 5% for all 5 gives 1276.28.

concepts.title: Nominal Rates & the Force of Interest
concepts.tagline: Same interest, different clothing. Convert between nominal, effective, and continuous so a rate never trips you up.

sections.body: Read this sentence slowly: **"12% compounded monthly" does not grow your money by 12% a year.** It grows it by 12.68%. The SOA quotes rates this way on purpose, because a student who blindly plugs 12% into an accumulation factor gets a wrong answer that *looks* reasonable. This concept is about never being fooled — learning to translate any rate (nominal, effective, force of interest, discount rate) into any other, so the wording can never trip you. Get fluent here and an entire genre of trap questions simply dissolves.

sections.title: A nominal rate is a label, not the real growth
sections.body:
An **effective** rate is honest: 6% effective means your money is exactly 6% bigger after one year, full stop. A **nominal** rate is a *label that hides a schedule.* When someone says "12% compounded monthly," the 12% is not the yearly growth — it is an annual headline you must first divide by 12 to get the *real* monthly rate of 1%, which then compounds twelve times.

Here is the key intuition: because that 1% earns interest-on-interest twelve times over the year, you end up with slightly *more* than 12%. Compounding more often always squeezes out a little extra growth. Quarterly beats annual, monthly beats quarterly, daily beats monthly — each by a shrinking margin. Push that frequency to its absolute limit — compounding every instant — and you reach the smooth ceiling called the **force of interest** $\delta$. So all four rate types describe the *same* growth from different angles, and the whole skill is converting between them.

sections.title: Deriving the nominal-to-effective bridge
sections.body: Let's build the conversion instead of memorizing it. A nominal rate $i^{(m)}$ compounds $m$ times a year. Step 1: find the *real* rate per compounding period — split the label evenly: $$\text{rate per period} = \frac{i^{(m)}}{m}.$$ Step 2: that small rate compounds $m$ times across the year, so by the accumulation logic you already know, one dollar becomes $\left(1 + \frac{i^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m$. Step 3: the **effective** annual rate $i$ is *by definition* whatever single yearly growth matches that, so set them equal: $$1 + i = \left(1 + \frac{i^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m.$$ That is the bridge — and notice it is just "find the period rate, then compound it $m$ times." There is nothing to memorize once you see where each piece comes from.

sections.title: The force of interest as the limit of compounding faster
sections.body:
What happens as we compound not 12 or 365 but *infinitely* often? Take $m \to \infty$ in the bridge above. A classic limit from calculus says $\left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^m \to e^{r}$, so the growth factor approaches $e^{\delta}$ where $\delta$ is the continuous (instantaneous) rate. Matching to the effective rate: $$1 + i = e^{\delta} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \delta = \ln(1+i).$$ This $\delta$ is the **force of interest** — the rate at which money grows at a single instant. To accumulate continuously over $t$ years you simply use $e^{\delta t}$.

And one cousin you must know: the **discount rate** $d$ is interest charged *in advance* rather than in arrears. If you borrow \$1 and immediately pay the year's interest $d$, you receive only $1-d$ today but owe \$1 in a year. That makes $1-d$ the present-value factor, i.e. $1 - d = v = \frac{1}{1+i}$, which rearranges to $$d = \frac{i}{1+i} = iv.$$ Four faces — $i$, $i^{(m)}$, $\delta$, $d$ — of one underlying growth.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — translate a nominal rate three ways
sections.body: A rate is quoted as 12% compounded monthly. Find the effective annual rate, the force of interest, and the annual effective discount rate. This single example exercises every bridge above.
steps: **Real monthly rate:** divide the label — $0.12/12 = 0.01$ (a true 1% per month).
**Effective annual:** compound it twelve times — $1 + i = (1.01)^{12} = 1.126825$, so $i = 12.68\%$. (Bigger than the 12% label, exactly as predicted.)
**Force of interest:** $\delta = \ln(1+i) = \ln(1.126825) = 0.11938$, i.e. $\delta \approx 11.94\%$.
**Sanity-check the ordering:** $d < \delta < i^{(12)} < i$, that is $11.26\% < 11.94\% < 12\% < 12.68\%$. They all describe the *same* growth; only the vantage point changes.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — match two nominal rates
sections.body: A trickier exam staple: find the nominal rate $i^{(4)}$ (compounded quarterly) equivalent to a nominal rate of 8% compounded monthly. You cannot convert nominal-to-nominal directly — route through the effective rate, the common currency.
steps: **Effective to quarterly nominal:** now invert the bridge. We need $\left(1 + \frac{i^{(4)}}{4}\right)^4 = 1.08300$, so $1 + \frac{i^{(4)}}{4} = 1.08300^{1/4} = 1.02016$.
**Answer:** $i^{(4)} \approx 8.06\%$. The recipe never changes — *anything-to-effective, then effective-to-anything.*

sections.title: Make the effective rate your home base
sections.body: Never convert one nominal rate straight to another, and never juggle $\delta$ and $d$ in the same breath — you will slip. Instead, *always land on the effective annual rate $i$ first.* It is the hub of a wheel: from $i$ you reach any nominal rate via $\left(1+\tfrac{i^{(m)}}{m}\right)^m = 1+i$, the force via $\delta = \ln(1+i)$, and the discount rate via $d = iv$ — each a single, memorized-once step. Two conversions through the hub is faster and far safer than one clever shortcut you'll fumble under time pressure.

sections.title: Three lookalike rates, three different jobs
sections.body: The force $\delta$ is **not** a nominal rate — do not divide it by $m$ and compound. Continuous growth over $t$ years is $e^{\delta t}$, period. Second, never confuse the discount rate $d$ with the discount *factor* $v$: $d$ is the interest you pay *in advance* (a rate), while $v$ is the present value of \$1 (a factor). They are linked by $v = 1 - d$, **not** $v = d$. Third, the nominal label is never the growth — "$i^{(m)} = 12\%$" means 1% twelve times, giving 12.68%, not 12%. Mix any of these up and you get a confident, plausible, wrong answer — which is exactly the trap the examiners set.

cards.front: Why is the effective rate always larger than the nominal rate it came from?
cards.back: Because the nominal label is split into $m$ equal pieces that each earn interest-on-interest as they compound $m$ times — that extra compounding adds growth beyond the bare label.

cards.front: Where does $\delta = \ln(1+i)$ come from?
cards.back: It's the limit of compounding infinitely often: $(1+i^{(m)}/m)^m \to e^{\delta}$ as $m\to\infty$, so $1+i = e^{\delta}$. Continuous accumulation over $t$ years is then $e^{\delta t}$.

questions.q: A nominal rate of 8% compounded quarterly has what effective annual rate?
If the effective annual rate is 6%, what is the force of interest $\delta$?
The force of interest is a constant $\delta = 0.05$. What is \$1000 worth after 10 years?
If $d = 0.05$ (annual effective discount rate), what is the effective interest rate $i$?
Which ordering is always correct for the same underlying annual growth?
questions.explain: More frequent compounding needs a smaller nominal label for the same effective $i$, and continuous needs the smallest of all: $\delta < i^{(m)} < i$.

questions.q: A nominal annual interest rate of 9% is compounded monthly. Calculate the equivalent annual effective interest rate.
questions.explain: $i = \left(1 + \frac{0.09}{12}\right)^{12} - 1 = (1.0075)^{12} - 1 = 0.0938 = 9.38\%$. The 9.00% answer mistakes the nominal label for the effective rate; effective always exceeds nominal when compounding more than once a year.

questions.q: The force of interest is $\delta_t = 0.04 + 0.01t$. Calculate the accumulated value at time 3 of 1 invested at time 0.
questions.explain: $\text{AV} = \exp\!\left(\int_0^3 (0.04 + 0.01t)\,dt\right) = \exp\!\left(0.04(3) + 0.01\cdot\frac{3^2}{2}\right) = \exp(0.12 + 0.045) = e^{0.165} = 1.1794$. Using only the constant part $e^{0.12}$, or forgetting to integrate the $0.01t$ term, gives the off answers.

concepts.title: The Equation of Value
concepts.tagline: Every FM problem is one idea: move all cash flows to a common date and set what comes in equal to what goes out. Master this and the whole exam is bookkeeping.

sections.body: If you internalize one idea on this whole exam, make it this: **there is only one FM problem, and it is the equation of value.** Drag every cash flow — in and out — to a single chosen date, then demand that the two sides balance. A loan is this. An annuity is this. A bond, a sinking fund, an immunized portfolio — all this, with different cash-flow shapes poured into the same mold. Every later concept is a *special case* of what you learn here. So when a future topic feels new, it isn't: find the cash flows, pick a date, write the balance.

sections.title: Dollars at different dates live in different time zones
sections.body:
You cannot add \$100 at time 2 to \$100 at time 5 any more than you can add 100 dollars to 100 euros — they are different units until you convert. *Time* is the exchange rate, and interest is the conversion factor. To make cash flows comparable you translate them all to one **valuation date**: anything earlier than that date gets pushed *forward* by $(1+i)^{t}$, anything later gets pulled *back* by $v^{t}$. Once every dollar sits on the same date, they are finally the same currency — now you may add them and set inflows equal to outflows.

The quietly powerful part: the valuation date is *yours to choose*, and the equation is true at **every** date simultaneously. That freedom is a gift you will exploit constantly to kill algebra before it starts.

sections.title: The master equation — and why the date doesn't matter
sections.body:
Pick a valuation date $T$. Translate each cash flow to $T$ and balance: $$\sum (\text{inflows})\,(1+i)^{\,T-t} = \sum (\text{outflows})\,(1+i)^{\,T-t}.$$ Equivalently, sign every cash flow (in $+$, out $-$) and demand the **net present value** vanish at the yield rate: $$\text{NPV}(i) = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t} = 0.$$

**Why is the date free?** Suppose the equation balances at date $T$. Move to a different date $T' = T + k$. Every single term — both sides — gets multiplied by the *same* extra factor $(1+i)^{k}$. Multiplying both sides of a true equation by the same number keeps it true. So if it balances at one date it balances at all of them. That is not a convenience; it's a theorem, and it's what lets you pick the *cleverest* date every time.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — solve for an unknown payment
sections.body: You deposit \$1000 now and \$2000 in 2 years. In exchange you receive \$X in 4 years. At $i = 6\%$, find the $X$ that makes the deal fair. Watch how choosing the date at $t=4$ keeps $X$ clean.
steps: **Choose the smart date:** value everything at $t=4$, where $X$ lives — that leaves $X$ with no discount factor attached.
**Accumulate the two deposits forward to $t=4$:** the \$1000 grows 4 years, the \$2000 grows 2 years. Balance: $1000(1.06)^4 + 2000(1.06)^2 = X$.

**Verify with a different date:** value everything at $t=0$ instead — $1000 + 2000v^2 = Xv^4$ gives $1000 + 1779.99 = X(0.79209)$, so $X = 2779.99/0.79209 = 3509.68$. Same answer, as the theorem promised.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — solve for the unknown yield
sections.body: Sometimes the *rate* is the unknown and the equation can't be solved by clean algebra — you bracket and close in. You pay \$1000 today and receive \$600 at $t=1$ and \$600 at $t=2$. Find the yield $i$.
steps: **Recognize it's a quadratic in $v$:** $600v^2 + 600v - 1000 = 0$, or $3v^2 + 3v - 5 = 0$.
**Quadratic formula:** $v = \dfrac{-3 + \sqrt{9 + 60}}{6} = \dfrac{-3 + \sqrt{69}}{6} = \dfrac{-3 + 8.3066}{6} = 0.88444$ (take the positive root).
**When it isn't a tidy quadratic** (three or more uneven flows), use the calculator's IRR or trial-and-error: pick two rates that make NPV straddle zero, then interpolate.

sections.title: Choose the date that erases the most work
sections.body: Since the equation holds at every date, *spend* that freedom. Two reliable moves: (1) **Put the date on top of an unknown payment** so that term carries no discount or accumulation factor — the unknown pops out with one division, as in Worked Example 1. (2) **Choose $t=0$** when you want every term to be a clean present value (natural for NPV and yield problems). The only 'wrong' date is the one that buries your unknown under the ugliest exponent. Glance at where the unknown sits, then anchor the date there.

sections.title: Unit mismatches and sign slips sink confident students
sections.body: Two silent killers. **(1) Period mismatch:** the rate and the exponent must share a time unit. A monthly cash flow needs a monthly rate (or convert time to years) — never an annual rate with a monthly count. **(2) Sign discipline:** decide once that inflows are $+$ and outflows are $-$ (or put them on opposite sides) and *stay consistent.* Tagging a deposit and a withdrawal with the same sign silently double-counts or cancels cash, and the equation still 'solves' — to a clean, plausible, wrong number. Before solving, eyeball your timeline: are the signs telling the real story of who pays whom?

cards.front: Why does the equation of value hold at every valuation date, not just $t=0$?
cards.back: Shifting the date multiplies *both* sides by the same factor $(1+i)^k$; multiplying a true equation by the same number keeps it true. So you may anchor the date wherever the algebra is cleanest.

cards.front: What's the smart valuation date when solving for an unknown payment?
cards.back: Put the date right on the unknown's payment time — then that term has no discount/accumulation factor and the unknown drops out with a single division.

questions.q: At $i = 8\%$ effective, what single payment today is equivalent to \$800 received in 3 years?
Deposits of \$1000 at $t=0$ and \$1000 at $t=1$ accumulate to what at $t=2$, $i=5\%$?
An investment pays \$300 at $t=1$ and \$300 at $t=2$. At $i=10\%$, its present value is closest to:
At what date may the equation of value be written?
choices: Only at the final cash-flow date
questions.explain: Both sides accumulate by the same factor, so the equation holds at every date — choose the most convenient.

questions.q: You borrow \$5000 today and repay \$2000 at $t=1$ and \$Y$ at $t=2$. At $i=6\%$, find $Y$.
A loan of 1000 is repaid by a payment of 600 at the end of year 1 and a payment of $X$ at the end of year 2. At 10% annual effective interest, calculate $X$.
questions.explain: Equation of value at $t=0$: $1000 = \frac{600}{1.1} + \frac{X}{1.1^2}$. So $\frac{X}{1.21} = 1000 - 545.45 = 454.55$, giving $X = 454.55(1.21) = 550.00$. Ignoring interest entirely ($1000-600+$ adjustments) leads to the distractors.

questions.q: Deposits of 100 are made at times 0, 1, and 2. At 6% annual effective interest, calculate the accumulated value of the fund at time 5.
questions.explain: Accumulate each deposit to time 5: $100\big[(1.06)^5 + (1.06)^4 + (1.06)^3\big] = 100(1.338226 + 1.262477 + 1.191016) = 379.17$. The 300.00 answer forgets to accumulate the deposits with interest.

modules.title: Annuities
modules.blurb: Level and varying streams of payments — the workhorse of FM. Annuity-immediate vs due, accumulated values, perpetuities, and increasing/decreasing annuities. The biggest standalone topic on the exam.

concepts.title: Level Annuities
concepts.tagline: A stream of equal payments collapses to one clean formula. The only real question is timing: immediate or due?

sections.body: A loan, a pension, a savings plan, a mortgage — strip away the story and each is the same object: a **level annuity**, the same payment landing period after period. You *could* discount thirty payments one at a time, but that's thirty chances to fumble. Instead, one short formula prices the entire stream at once — and that formula isn't magic, it's a geometric series you can rebuild from scratch in ten seconds. Nail two things here, the formula's *origin* and the *timing* (do payments fall at the end or start of each period?), and annuities become the easiest big topic on the exam.

sections.title: Immediate pays in arrears; due pays in advance
sections.body:
Two flavors, one tiny difference. An **annuity-immediate** pays at the *end* of each period — the way you repay a loan, *after* you've had use of the money. An **annuity-due** pays at the *start* of each period — the way you pay rent, *before* you occupy the apartment. That's the whole distinction.

And it has a clean consequence: every due payment arrives exactly one period *earlier* than the matching immediate payment, so it has dodged one period of discounting and is worth a factor of $(1+i)$ more. Multiply the entire immediate annuity by $(1+i)$ and you've shifted every payment one step earlier — that's the due annuity. You will never memorize a separate due formula; you'll *nudge* the immediate one.

sections.title: Deriving the annuity formula from a geometric series
sections.body: Picture \$1 at the end of each year for $n$ years, discounted to today. The present value is literally the sum of each payment's discount factor: $$a_{\overline{n}|} = v + v^2 + v^3 + \cdots + v^n.$$ That is a **geometric series** — first term $v$, common ratio $v$. The standard sum of such a series is $\text{first}\times\frac{1 - \text{ratio}^{\text{count}}}{1 - \text{ratio}}$: $$a_{\overline{n}|} = v\cdot\frac{1 - v^n}{1 - v}.$$ Now simplify the denominator — this is the satisfying step. Since $v = \frac{1}{1+i}$, we get $1 - v = 1 - \frac{1}{1+i} = \frac{i}{1+i} = iv$. Substituting, the $v$ on top cancels the $v$ inside $1-v$: $$a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{v(1 - v^n)}{iv} = \frac{1 - v^n}{i}.$$ **There it is.** Not memorized — *derived.* The accumulated value is the same series valued at the last payment instead of today: $s_{\overline{n}|} = 1 + (1+i) + \cdots + (1+i)^{n-1} = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i}$. And the due versions are just the $(1+i)$ nudge: $\ddot{a}_{\overline{n}|} = (1+i)\,a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{1-v^n}{d}$, $\ddot{s}_{\overline{n}|} = (1+i)\,s_{\overline{n}|}$.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — price a 10-year stream
sections.body: Find the present value of \$500 paid at the end of each year for 10 years at 6% effective.
steps: **Identify the type:** payments at year-end → annuity-immediate, PV $= 500\,a_{\overline{10}|}$.
**Scale by the payment:** PV $= 500 \times 7.3601 = \$3680.04$.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — solve for the payment (a real loan)
sections.body: The annuity formula runs backwards just as easily. You borrow \$20{,}000 to be repaid by equal end-of-year payments over 5 years at 7%. Find the annual payment $P$ — this is exactly how a bank sets a loan installment.
steps: **The loan IS an annuity:** the bank pays you \$20{,}000 today in exchange for your stream of $P$, so $20{,}000 = P\,a_{\overline{5}|}$.
**Divide to isolate the payment:** $P = \dfrac{20{,}000}{4.1002} = \$4877.81$.
**Gut-check:** five payments of ~\$4878 total \$24{,}389; the \$4389 excess over \$20{,}000 is the interest — plausible for 7% over 5 years.

sections.title: Memorize one factor, nudge for the rest
sections.body: Don't carry four formulas in your head — carry one and a move. Compute the **immediate** present value $a_{\overline{n}|}$, then: multiply by $(1+i)$ to get the **due** value (every payment shifted one period earlier); the accumulated value is the same number pushed to the end, $s_{\overline{n}|} = (1+i)^n\,a_{\overline{n}|}$. So $a_{\overline{n}|}$ is your home base and everything else is one multiplication away. Under exam pressure, fewer memorized objects means fewer ways to be wrong.

sections.title: Where is the annuity actually valued?
sections.body: Every annuity symbol has a *built-in valuation date*, and forgetting it costs a clean $(1+i)$. $a_{\overline{n}|}$ is valued **one period before the first payment** (i.e. 'today' for an immediate annuity). $s_{\overline{n}|}$ is valued at the **moment of the last payment** — so if a problem asks for the balance one period *after* the final deposit, you still owe another $(1+i)$. And the perennial slip: pricing an annuity-due with the immediate formula, dropping a full $(1+i)$. Defense is always the same — sketch the timeline, mark where payments land, mark the date the question wants, and count the gap.

cards.front: Reconstruct $a_{\overline{n}|}$ from scratch — what series is it and what does it sum to?
cards.back: It's the geometric series $v + v^2 + \cdots + v^n = v\frac{1-v^n}{1-v}$; since $1-v = iv$, this simplifies to $(1-v^n)/i$.

cards.front: Why is an annuity-due worth $(1+i)$ times the immediate one?
cards.back: Every due payment lands one period earlier, escaping one period of discounting — so each is worth a factor of $(1+i)$ more, and so is the whole stream.

questions.q: Find the present value of \$1000 paid at the end of each year for 5 years at 8% effective.
What is the accumulated value at the end of 5 years of \$200 deposited at the end of each year, at 6%?
If $a_{\overline{n}|} = 7.36$ at $i = 6\%$, what is the corresponding annuity-due value $\ddot{a}_{\overline{n}|}$?
A savings plan deposits \$300 at the START of each year for 10 years at 5%. Accumulated value at end of year 10?
The present value of an $n$-year annuity-immediate of 1 is 8.5 at rate $i$, and $v^n = 0.49$. Find $i$.
questions.explain: $a_{\overline{n}|} = (1 - v^n)/i \Rightarrow 8.5 = (1 - 0.49)/i = 0.51/i \Rightarrow i = 0.06 = 6\%$.

questions.q: A loan of 10000 is repaid with level payments at the end of each year for 10 years at 7% annual effective interest. Calculate the annual payment.
questions.explain: Payment $= \frac{10000}{a_{\overline{10}|0.07}}$. Here $a_{\overline{10}|} = \frac{1 - 1.07^{-10}}{0.07} = 7.02358$, so payment $= \frac{10000}{7.02358} = 1423.78$. Dividing principal by 10 (ignoring interest) gives 1000.

questions.q: Deposits of 500 are made at the BEGINNING of each year for 8 years into an account earning 5% annual effective interest. Calculate the accumulated value at the end of year 8.
questions.explain: Beginning-of-year deposits form an annuity-due: $500 \cdot \ddot{s}_{\overline{8}|0.05} = 500 \cdot s_{\overline{8}|}(1.05) = 500(9.54911)(1.05) = 5013.28$. Treating them as end-of-year (annuity-immediate) drops the $(1.05)$ factor and gives 4774.55.

concepts.title: Perpetuities & Varying Annuities
concepts.tagline: Payments forever, or payments that grow. The shortcuts here turn intimidating streams into one-line answers.

sections.body: Now the payments stop being polite. Some streams run *forever* (perpetuities — endowments, consols, dividend-paying stocks); some *climb* every year (increasing annuities — pensions with cost-of-living bumps). They look like infinite sums you could never add by hand, and that's exactly the point: each collapses to a one-line closed form, and the exam pays you handsomely for recognizing the pattern on sight. The secret is that every one of these is *still* a geometric series — you already own the machinery.

sections.title: Why 'forever' costs a finite, small amount
sections.body:
It feels paradoxical that paying \$1 every year *for eternity* has a finite price — but discounting is relentless. The payment in year 50 is worth $v^{50}$; in year 100, $v^{100}$ — vanishingly small. The far tail of the stream contributes almost nothing, so the infinite sum *converges*. Concretely, at 5% a perpetuity of \$1 forever is worth just $1/0.05 = \$20$ today. Twenty dollars buys an infinite stream, because by year 100 each dollar is worth less than a penny in today's money.

Increasing streams add a second moving part — the payment size grows while the discount shrinks it — and the closed forms simply bookkeep that tug-of-war between growth and discounting.

sections.title: Deriving the perpetuity from the annuity limit
sections.body:
Don't memorize $1/i$ — *take a limit.* A perpetuity-immediate is an annuity-immediate with $n \to \infty$: $$\frac{1}{i}\text{-perpetuity} = \lim_{n\to\infty} a_{\overline{n}|} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1 - v^n}{i}.$$ Since $|v| < 1$, $v^n \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, leaving $$a_{\overline{\infty}|} = \frac{1 - 0}{i} = \frac{1}{i}.$$ Clean. The perpetuity-**due** lands one period earlier, so multiply by $(1+i)$: $\frac{1+i}{i} = \frac{1}{d}$.

**Increasing perpetuity** (payments $1, 2, 3, \dots$ forever): here's the slick derivation. Think of it as *layers* of level perpetuities. A \$1 perpetuity starting year 1 is worth $1/i$. Another \$1 perpetuity starting year 2 (worth $\frac{1}{i}\cdot v$ today) stacks on top. Another starting year 3, and so on. Summing those layers, $\frac{1}{i}(1 + v + v^2 + \cdots) = \frac{1}{i}\cdot\frac{1}{1-v} = \frac{1}{i}\cdot\frac{1}{iv} = \frac{1}{i^2}\cdot\frac{1}{v}$... cleaner to state the standard result: $$(I a)_{\overline{\infty}|} = \frac{1}{i} + \frac{1}{i^2} = \frac{i+1}{i^2}.$$ For the *finite* increasing annuity, $(Ia)_{\overline{n}|} = \dfrac{\ddot{a}_{\overline{n}|} - n v^n}{i}$.

sections.title: The geometrically-growing perpetuity — derive 1/(i−g)
sections.body: This one is a dividend-model workhorse, so derive it once and own it. Payments grow by a factor $(1+g)$ each year: first payment 1 at year 1, then $(1+g)$, then $(1+g)^2$, .... Present value: $$PV = v + (1+g)v^2 + (1+g)^2 v^3 + \cdots$$ Factor out $v$: $PV = v\left[1 + (1+g)v + ((1+g)v)^2 + \cdots\right]$ — a geometric series with ratio $r = (1+g)v$. It sums (when $r<1$, i.e. $g<i$) to $\frac{1}{1-r}$: $$PV = \frac{v}{1 - (1+g)v}.$$ Multiply top and bottom by $(1+i)$ (recall $v=\frac{1}{1+i}$): $$PV = \frac{1}{(1+i) - (1+g)} = \frac{1}{i - g}.$$ So the famous $\frac{1}{i-g}$ isn't a separate fact — it's the geometric-series sum in disguise. Valid only when $i > g$; if growth outran the discount rate the sum would diverge.

sections.title: Worked example — a growing-dividend valuation
sections.body: A perpetuity pays \$100 at the end of year 1, \$200 at year 2, \$300 at year 3, and so on forever (arithmetic growth). At $i = 10\%$, find its present value.
steps: **Recognize the shape:** payments $100, 200, 300, \dots$ are $100\times(1, 2, 3, \dots)$ — that's 100 copies of an increasing perpetuity-immediate with base 1.
**Apply the derived increasing-perpetuity formula:** per unit, $\dfrac{1}{i} + \dfrac{1}{i^2} = \dfrac{1}{0.1} + \dfrac{1}{0.01} = 10 + 100 = 110$.
**Don't confuse arithmetic with geometric growth:** payments $+\$100$ each year is *arithmetic* (use $Ia$); payments $\times 1.10$ each year would be *geometric* (use $1/(i-g)$).

sections.title: Split any messy stream into level + increasing layers
sections.body: A stream like "\$500 in year 1, then rising \$100 a year" looks custom, but it's two familiar pieces glued together: a **level** annuity of \$400 forever-or-$n$-years, *plus* an **increasing** annuity $(Ia)$ with base \$100 (giving $400+100=500$ in year 1, $400+200=600$ in year 2, ...). Price each layer with its own closed form and add. This decompose-and-add move cracks the large majority of varying-annuity questions — whenever a stream resists one formula, look for the level part hiding inside it.

sections.title: Immediate vs due, and arithmetic vs geometric growth
sections.body: Two traps live here. **(1) Perpetuity timing:** immediate is $1/i$, due is $1/d$ — pick wrong and you drop a $(1+i)$. **(2) Growth type:** "increases by \$50 each year" is *arithmetic* → use $(Ia)$ / the $1/i+1/i^2$ family; "increases by 5% each year" is *geometric* → use $1/(i-g)$. They are completely different formulas, and the words 'by \$X' versus 'by X%' are your only clue. Read that phrase twice before choosing. And for $1/(i-g)$, sanity-check $i>g$ — otherwise the stream has no finite value.

cards.front: Why does a perpetuity's value $1/i$ fall out of the annuity formula?
cards.back: It's $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{\overline{n}|} = \lim (1-v^n)/i$; since $v^n\to 0$, it collapses to $1/i$. The infinite tail is discounted to nothing.

cards.front: Where does the dividend-model $1/(i-g)$ come from?
cards.back: It's the sum of the geometric series $v + (1+g)v^2 + \cdots$ with ratio $(1+g)v$; summing and simplifying gives $1/(i-g)$, valid for $i>g$.

questions.q: A perpetuity pays \$50 at the end of each year forever. At 5% effective, find its present value.
questions.explain: Perpetuity-immediate: $50/0.05 = 1000$.

questions.q: A perpetuity-due pays \$100 per year at 8%. Find its present value.
A stock pays \$4 next year, growing 3% annually forever. At a 9% discount rate, find the price.
An increasing perpetuity pays \$10, \$20, \$30, ... at year-ends forever, at 5%. Find its present value.
A perpetuity pays 1000 at the end of each year, with the FIRST payment at the end of year 6. At 8% annual effective interest, calculate the present value.
questions.explain: Value the perpetuity one period before its first payment (at time 5), then discount to today: $\frac{1000}{0.08}\cdot v^5 = 12500(1.08^{-5}) = 12500(0.680583) = 8507.29$. No discount gives 12500; discounting by $v^4$ or $v^6$ gives the other distractors.

questions.q: A perpetuity-immediate pays 100 at the end of year 1, 200 at the end of year 2, and increases by 100 each year forever. At 10% annual effective interest, calculate the present value.
questions.explain: An increasing perpetuity-immediate has PV $= \frac{1+i}{i^2}$ per unit of increase: $100\cdot\frac{1.10}{0.10^2} = 100(110) = 11000$. Using $\frac{1}{i^2}$ (forgetting the $(1+i)$ numerator) gives 10000.

concepts.title: Deferred & Continuous Annuities
concepts.tagline: Push a level annuity into the future with one discount factor, or let the payments flow continuously and integrate. Two variations the exam tests cleanly.

sections.body: Two natural twists on the level annuity, and both are *less* work than they look. A **deferred** annuity simply doesn't start paying for a while — a pension that kicks in at retirement, a loan with a grace period. A **continuous** annuity pays in an unbroken trickle instead of discrete lumps — the idealized limit of paying weekly, then daily, then every instant. Here's the reassuring truth: neither is a new formula to memorize. Each is the *level annuity you already own*, multiplied by exactly one extra factor. Learn which factor, and why, and these become free points.

sections.title: Defer = value at its own start, then slide it back
sections.body:
A deferred annuity isn't a different creature — it's an ordinary annuity that you're looking at *early*. So value it the lazy way: pretend it starts now, price it with the plain formula, then **drag that single lump sum back** across the deferral gap with one discount factor $v^m$. The annuity doesn't care from which date you observe it; you value it where it naturally lives (one period before its first payment) and then discount that value to today.

The **continuous** annuity comes from a different limit. Pay \$1/year as 12 monthly bits, then 365 daily bits, then infinitely many infinitesimal bits — the discrete sum $\sum v^t$ smooths into the integral $\int_0^n v^t\,dt$. Integration is just summation taken to the continuous limit, and it produces a tidy closed form.

sections.title: Deriving the continuous annuity by integration
sections.body:
**Deferred** first (the easy one). An $m$-year deferred, $n$-payment annuity-immediate is value-then-discount: $$_{m|}a_{\overline{n}|} = v^m\, a_{\overline{n}|}.$$ There's also a slick subtraction identity — a full $(m+n)$-year annuity minus the first $m$ years you don't actually receive: $_{m|}a_{\overline{n}|} = a_{\overline{m+n}|} - a_{\overline{m}|}$. Same number, two viewpoints.

**Continuous**, derived from scratch. Sum (integrate) the discount factor over the payment window: $$\bar a_{\overline{n}|} = \int_0^n v^t\,dt.$$ Write $v^t = e^{t\ln v} = e^{-\delta t}$ (since $\ln v = -\ln(1+i) = -\delta$). The integral of $e^{-\delta t}$ is $-\frac{1}{\delta}e^{-\delta t}$, so $$\bar a_{\overline{n}|} = \left[-\frac{e^{-\delta t}}{\delta}\right]_0^n = \frac{1 - e^{-\delta n}}{\delta} = \frac{1 - v^n}{\delta}.$$ Notice the result is the *spitting image* of $a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{1-v^n}{i}$ — only the denominator changed from $i$ to the **force** $\delta$. The continuous analogue of the period rate is the instantaneous rate. Accumulated version: $\bar s_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{\delta}$.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — a deferred annuity
sections.body: An annuity pays \$1000 at the end of each year for 10 years, but the first payment is at the end of year 6 (a 5-year deferral). At $i = 7\%$, find the present value. Use $a_{\overline{10}|} = 7.0236$.
steps: **Where does the plain formula plant the value?** $a_{\overline{10}|}$ values the stream one period before its first payment. First payment is at $t=6$, so the formula's value sits at $t=5$.
**Value it there:** $1000\,a_{\overline{10}|} = 1000(7.0236) = 7023.60$, a lump sum located at $t=5$.
**Slide it back 5 years:** $\times v^5 = (1.07)^{-5} = 0.71299$.
**Result:** $PV = 7023.60 \times 0.71299 = \$5008.7$. (The deferral exponent is 5, not 6 — that off-by-one is the whole game.)

sections.title: Worked example 2 — continuous annuity, then the i/δ shortcut
sections.body: A continuous annuity pays at rate \$1/year for 5 years at $i = 7\%$ effective ($\delta = \ln 1.07 = 0.06766$). Find $\bar a_{\overline{5}|}$ directly, then show it equals $\frac{i}{\delta}a_{\overline{5}|}$.
steps: **Via the shortcut:** the discrete $a_{\overline{5}|} = \dfrac{1 - 0.71299}{0.07} = 4.1002$.
**Why slightly bigger than discrete?** A continuous stream delivers money a touch *earlier* within each year, so its PV exceeds the year-end annuity by exactly the factor $i/\delta > 1$.

sections.title: Two reusable conversion factors
sections.body: Don't re-derive — convert. (1) **Continuous from discrete:** $\bar a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{i}{\delta}\,a_{\overline{n}|}$. Already have the discrete annuity factor? One multiply by $i/\delta$ and you're done — no integral needed. Because $i > \delta$, expect a slightly larger number. (2) **Deferred from plain:** value the annuity at its natural start, then multiply by $v^{(\text{deferral})}$. Both moves reduce a scary-looking variant to your level-annuity home base plus a single factor.

sections.title: The deferral exponent is one less than you think
sections.body: The signature deferred-annuity mistake is an off-by-one on the discount power. The annuity-immediate formula *already* values the stream **one period before the first payment** — that's baked in. So if the first payment is at time $m+1$, the formula's value sits at time $m$, and you discount by $v^{m}$, **not** $v^{m+1}$. Equivalently: count the number of *empty* periods before the formula's valuation point, not before the first payment. Always sketch the timeline, mark where the plain formula 'plants its flag,' and count the gap from there to today.

cards.front: Where does the continuous annuity formula $\frac{1-v^n}{\delta}$ come from?
cards.back: From $\int_0^n v^t dt = \int_0^n e^{-\delta t}dt = \frac{1-e^{-\delta n}}{\delta} = \frac{1-v^n}{\delta}$. It mirrors the discrete $\frac{1-v^n}{i}$ with $i$ replaced by the force $\delta$.

cards.front: First payment of a deferred annuity is at time $m+1$ — what's the discount exponent, and why?
cards.back: $v^m$. The immediate formula already values the stream at time $m$ (one period before the first payment), so you only discount $m$ more periods to today.

questions.q: A 4-year annuity-immediate of \$1 is deferred 3 years ($a_{\overline{4}|}=3.3872$ at 7%, $v^3=0.8163$). Find its present value.
A continuous annuity pays at rate \$1/year for 5 years. If $\delta=0.06$ and $v^5=0.7408$, find $\bar a_{\overline{5}|}$.
Given $a_{\overline{n}|}=8.0$, $i=0.06$, $\delta=0.0583$, find the continuous annuity $\bar a_{\overline{n}|}$.
An annuity's first of 10 annual payments occurs at $t=6$. By what factor do you discount the standard $a_{\overline{10}|}$ value?
questions.explain: The immediate formula values the annuity at $t=5$ (one period before the first payment at $t=6$), so discount by $v^5$.

questions.q: Why is a continuous annuity worth more than the otherwise-identical annuity-immediate?
choices: It is not — they are equal
questions.explain: A continuous stream effectively delivers money earlier within each period, so its PV is larger by the factor $i/\delta>1$.

questions.q: Payments are made continuously at a rate of 1000 per year for 5 years. At a constant force of interest $\delta = 0.06$, calculate the present value.
questions.explain: Continuous annuity: $\bar{a}_{\overline{5}|} = \frac{1 - v^5}{\delta} = \frac{1 - e^{-0.06(5)}}{0.06} = \frac{1 - 0.740818}{0.06} = 4.31970$, so PV $= 1000(4.31970) = 4319.70$. Using $5$ years undiscounted gives 5000.

questions.q: An annuity-immediate pays 2000 per year for 10 years, but the first payment is at the end of year 4 (deferred 3 years). At 6% annual effective interest, calculate the present value.
questions.explain: Value the 10-year annuity at its start (time 3), then discount: $2000\,a_{\overline{10}|0.06}\,v^3 = 2000(7.360087)(1.06^{-3}) = 2000(7.360087)(0.839619) = 12359.34$. Forgetting the 3-year deferral discount gives 14720.17.

concepts.title: Geometric (Growing) Annuities
concepts.tagline: Payments that grow by a fixed percentage each year — pensions with COLA, dividends. One adjusted-rate trick turns them back into a level annuity.

sections.body: Real money rarely stays flat. Salaries get cost-of-living raises, dividends grow, rents step up a fixed percentage every year. A **geometric annuity** is a stream where each payment is a constant *multiple* $(1+g)$ of the one before. It looks like a brand-new beast — but one clever change of rate collapses it right back into the level annuity you already know cold. The whole concept is a single trick: *fold the growth into the discount rate.*

sections.title: Growth and discounting are tug-of-war on the same rope
sections.body: Each year two things happen to a future payment. It *grows* by $(1+g)$ (good for you), and it gets *discounted* by another $(1+i)$ (shrinks its present value). Those two factors are fighting over the same payment, and what actually matters is the **net** of the two. So define a single **adjusted rate** $j$ that captures the net effect: $$1 + j = \frac{1+i}{1+g}.$$ Read it literally — you discount at $(1+i)$ but get $(1+g)$ of growth back, so the *effective* shrink-per-year is the ratio. Once you've defined $j$, a *growing* annuity at rate $i$ becomes a plain *level* annuity at rate $j$ (with a small rescaling). The intimidating topic reduces to: compute $j$, then use $a_{\overline{n}|}$ at $j$.

sections.title: Deriving the growing-annuity formula
sections.body: First payment \$1 at $t=1$, then growing by $(1+g)$ each year for $n$ payments, discounted at $i$. Write out the present value: $$PV = \frac{1}{1+i} + \frac{1+g}{(1+i)^2} + \cdots + \frac{(1+g)^{n-1}}{(1+i)^n}.$$ Factor $\frac{1}{1+i}$ from every term: $PV = \frac{1}{1+i}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\frac{1+g}{1+i}\right)^k$ — a geometric series with ratio $r = \frac{1+g}{1+i} = \frac{1}{1+j}$. Summing $\frac{1-r^n}{1-r}$ and simplifying (use $1 - r = 1 - \frac{1+g}{1+i} = \frac{i-g}{1+i}$) gives the clean closed form: $$PV = \frac{1 - \left(\frac{1+g}{1+i}\right)^n}{i - g}.$$ Let $n\to\infty$: if $i>g$ the ratio $r<1$ so $r^n\to 0$, leaving the famous **growing perpetuity** $$PV = \frac{1}{i-g}.$$ Equivalent calculator-friendly recipe: compute the level annuity $a_{\overline{n}|}$ at the adjusted rate $j$, then divide by $(1+g)$ — same answer, fewer keystrokes.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — a growing perpetuity (Gordon growth)
sections.body: A perpetuity pays \$100 at the end of year 1, growing 3% per year forever, discounted at 8%. Find its present value.
steps: **Identify it's geometric and infinite:** payments $\times 1.03$ each year, forever → growing-perpetuity formula.
**Apply $\frac{P_1}{i-g}$ with the first payment 100:** $PV = \dfrac{100}{0.08 - 0.03} = \dfrac{100}{0.05} = \$2000$.
**Sanity check against the level case:** a *flat* \$100 perpetuity at 8% is $100/0.08 = \$1250$; the 3% growth lifts it to \$2000. Growth makes it worth more — as it must.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — the adjusted-rate trick on a finite annuity
sections.body: A 20-year annuity pays \$1000 at the end of year 1, increasing 4% each year, discounted at 9%. Price it using the adjusted-rate method to show the trick in action.
steps: **Cross-check with the direct formula:** $\dfrac{1 - (1.04/1.09)^{20}}{0.09-0.04} = \dfrac{1 - 0.39157}{0.05} = \dfrac{0.60843}{0.05}\times\frac{1}{1.04}\cdots$ — same \$12{,}167. The trick and the formula are one and the same.

sections.title: Memorize Gordon growth; derive the rest from j
sections.body: Burn $\dfrac{P_1}{i-g}$ into memory — the **Gordon growth model** of finance — because dividend and pension questions hand it to you constantly, and it's a one-liner. For *finite* growing annuities, don't memorize the bulky formula; instead compute the adjusted rate $1+j=\frac{1+i}{1+g}$, treat the stream as a plain level annuity at $j$, and divide by $(1+g)$ at the end. One reusable move handles every geometric annuity the exam can throw at you.

sections.title: First payment, $i>g$, and percent-vs-dollar growth
sections.body: Three landmines. **(1)** In $\frac{P_1}{i-g}$, the numerator is the payment at $t=1$ — *not* a 'base' figure quoted before the first raise, and not a $t=0$ amount. Read the timeline. **(2)** The perpetuity needs $i>g$; if $g\ge i$ payments grow at least as fast as you discount and the value is infinite — the shortcut is meaningless (a finite growing *annuity* still works via the general formula). **(3)** Don't confuse this with arithmetic growth: "increases 4% a year" is geometric (this concept); "increases by \$40 a year" is arithmetic (use $Ia$). The single word percent-vs-dollars decides which formula you reach for.

cards.front: What single substitution turns a growing annuity into a level one, and why?
cards.back: The adjusted rate $1+j = \frac{1+i}{1+g}$ — it nets growth against discounting. Then value at $j$ as a level annuity and divide by $(1+g)$.

cards.front: Derive the growing-perpetuity value and state its condition.
cards.back: The PV is the geometric series $\frac{1}{1+i}\sum (\frac{1+g}{1+i})^k$; for $i>g$ the ratio <1 and it sums to $\frac{1}{i-g}$ (Gordon growth). If $g\ge i$ it diverges.

questions.q: A perpetuity pays \$200 in year 1, growing 4% yearly, discounted at 9%. Find its present value.
A dividend of \$5 next year grows 6% forever; the discount rate is 11%. Find the present value.
For a growing perpetuity, what condition must hold for a finite present value?
questions.explain: The series $\sum \frac{(1+g)^{t-1}}{(1+i)^t}$ converges only when $i>g$.

questions.q: A 3-payment annuity pays \$100, then grows 10% each year, discounted at 10%. Find the present value.
questions.explain: When $g=i$, each discounted payment equals $\frac{100}{1.1}=90.91$, and there are 3 of them: $3\times90.91=272.73$.

questions.q: The growing-perpetuity formula $\frac{P_1}{i-g}$ is also known in finance as the:
questions.explain: It is the Gordon growth (dividend discount) model.

questions.q: An annuity-immediate makes 10 annual payments. The first is 1000 and each later payment is 4% larger than the one before. At 9% annual effective interest, calculate the present value.
questions.explain: Geometric annuity: PV $= P\cdot\frac{1 - \left(\frac{1+g}{1+i}\right)^n}{i - g} = 1000\cdot\frac{1 - (1.04/1.09)^{10}}{0.09 - 0.04} = 1000\cdot\frac{1 - 0.62534}{0.05} = 7494.58$. Treating the payments as level (ignoring 4% growth) gives the level annuity 6417.66.

questions.q: A perpetuity-immediate pays 500 at the end of year 1 and grows 3% per year forever. At 8% annual effective interest, calculate the present value.
questions.explain: Growing perpetuity (Gordon): PV $= \frac{P}{i - g} = \frac{500}{0.08 - 0.03} = \frac{500}{0.05} = 10000$. Ignoring growth ($500/0.08$) gives 6250; dividing by $g$ instead of $i-g$ gives 16667.

modules.title: Loans
modules.blurb: Amortization and the split of each payment into interest and principal. Outstanding balance two ways — prospective and retrospective — and the sinking-fund alternative.

concepts.title: Loan Amortization
concepts.tagline: Every payment is part interest, part principal. The outstanding balance is just the present value of what is left to pay.

sections.body: Amortization questions are free points once one sentence lives in your bones: **the outstanding balance is the present value of the payments you still owe.** Not a schedule to grind through, not a balance to track row by row — just a present value of what remains. From that single anchor, every quantity the exam asks for (this month's interest, this month's principal, the balance after payment 17) falls out in two lines. We'll derive *why* each payment splits the way it does so you never have to memorize the split.

sections.title: Why early payments are almost all interest
sections.body: Each level payment $R$ does two jobs: first it pays the interest that just accrued on the balance, and whatever is left chips away at the principal. Early in the loan the balance is *huge*, so the interest it throws off is huge, and only a sliver of your payment touches principal. As principal slowly falls, the interest it generates falls too — so more of each fixed payment attacks principal, and the payoff accelerates. That's why your first mortgage payments feel like they barely move the balance: the principal-repayment curve is **back-loaded**, small at first and snowballing later. Crucially, the principal portions themselves grow by exactly $(1+i)$ each period — a fact we'll prove, and one the exam loves to test.

sections.title: Deriving the balance, interest, and principal split
sections.body:
**Balance (prospective).** The lender is owed exactly the present value of the remaining payments. After $t$ payments, $n-t$ payments of $R$ remain, so $$B_t = R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}.$$ That's the master equation of value applied to 'what's left' — nothing new.

**Interest in the next payment.** Interest accrues on the current balance for one period: $$I_{t+1} = i\,B_t.$$

**Principal in the next payment.** Whatever the payment doesn't spend on interest: $$P_{t+1} = R - I_{t+1} = R - i\,B_t.$$

**Why principal grows by $(1+i)$.** Here's the proof. $P_{t+1} = R - iB_t$ and $P_t = R - iB_{t-1}$. Subtract: $P_{t+1} - P_t = -i(B_t - B_{t-1}) = -i(-P_t) = iP_t$ (since the balance drops by exactly the principal paid). So $P_{t+1} = P_t + iP_t = (1+i)P_t$. Each principal repayment is the previous one grown by $(1+i)$ — a geometric ladder. Combined with $P_1 = R - iB_0 = R(1 - v^n)$, you can jump to *any* principal portion: $P_{t+1} = R\,v^{\,n-t}$.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — split a payment into interest and principal
sections.body: A \$10{,}000 loan at 8% is repaid with level annual payments over 5 years. Find the payment, then the interest and principal in payment 1.
steps: **Payment from the loan-as-annuity equation:** $10{,}000 = R\,a_{\overline{5}|}$ with $a_{\overline{5}|} = 3.9927$, so $R = 10{,}000/3.9927 = \$2504.56$.
**Interest in payment 1:** interest on the full starting balance, $I_1 = 0.08 \times 10{,}000 = \$800$.
**Principal in payment 1:** the leftover, $P_1 = 2504.56 - 800 = \$1704.56$.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — balance after several payments, two ways
sections.body: For the same \$10{,}000 / 8% / 5-year loan ($R = 2504.56$), find the outstanding balance just after payment 3, using both the prospective and retrospective methods to show they agree.
steps: **Prospective (PV of the 2 remaining payments):** $B_3 = R\,a_{\overline{2}|} = 2504.56 \times \dfrac{1 - 1.08^{-2}}{0.08} = 2504.56 \times 1.78326 = \$4466.4$.
**Retrospective (accumulate the loan, subtract accumulated payments):** $B_3 = 10{,}000(1.08)^3 - R\,s_{\overline{3}|} = 12{,}597.1 - 2504.56(3.2464) = 12{,}597.1 - 8130.8 = \$4466.3$.
**They match** (to rounding). Use whichever side has fewer terms — here prospective wins with only 2 payments left versus 3 behind.

sections.title: Prospective balance, then i×balance — the two-line solve
sections.body: Almost every amortization question yields to one reflex: get the balance as the PV of what's left, $B_t = R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}$, then the very next interest is $i\times B_t$ and the principal is the remainder $R - iB_t$. No row-by-row schedule, no accumulation grind. A companion shortcut for principal: since the portions form a geometric ladder, the principal in payment $t+1$ is $P_{t+1} = R\,v^{\,n-t}$ — letting you snipe a single year's principal without computing any balance at all.

sections.title: Prospective vs retrospective — and changed payments
sections.body: The **prospective** balance (PV of future payments) and the **retrospective** balance (accumulated loan minus accumulated payments) must always agree — they're the same equation of value seen from opposite ends. But the shortcut $B_t = R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}$ secretly assumes the payment $R$ and rate $i$ stay constant for the *whole* remaining term. The moment a loan has an irregular final payment, a payment holiday, or a rate change, that clean formula lies — you must rebuild from the actual remaining schedule. When a problem says 'the last payment is adjusted to exactly retire the loan,' that's your cue the simple formula no longer applies to the tail.

cards.front: Why does the outstanding balance equal $R\,a_{\overline{n-t}|}$?
cards.back: Because the lender is owed precisely the present value of the payments still to come — it's the equation of value applied to the remaining $n-t$ payments.

cards.front: Prove that successive principal repayments grow by $(1+i)$.
cards.back: $P_{t+1}-P_t = -i(B_t-B_{t-1}) = -i(-P_t) = iP_t$, so $P_{t+1}=(1+i)P_t$. The principal portions form a geometric ladder; equivalently $P_{t+1}=R\,v^{n-t}$.

questions.q: A \$20,000 loan at 6% is repaid with level annual payments over 10 years. Find the annual payment. ($a_{\overline{10}|} = 7.3601$)
For that same loan, how much interest is in the first payment?
A loan has level payments of \$500 with 6 payments remaining at 7%. What is the outstanding balance now? ($a_{\overline{6}|} = 4.7665$)
questions.explain: Prospective: $B = 500 \times a_{\overline{6}|} = 500(4.7665) = 2383$.

questions.q: If the principal repaid in the first payment of a 5-year loan is \$1704.56 at 8%, what is the principal repaid in the second payment?
questions.explain: Principal repayments grow by $(1+i)$: $1704.56 \times 1.08 = 1840.92$.

questions.q: A loan is repaid with 12 level payments. The interest in payment 1 is \$600 and the payment is \$1000. What is the original loan amount if $i = 6\%$?
questions.explain: $I_1 = i \times L \Rightarrow 600 = 0.06 L \Rightarrow L = 10000$.

questions.q: A loan is repaid with level annual payments of 1000 for 15 years at 8% annual effective interest. Calculate the outstanding balance immediately after the 8th payment.
questions.explain: Prospective method — outstanding balance equals the PV of the remaining payments. After the 8th of 15, there are 7 left: $1000\,a_{\overline{7}|0.08} = 1000(5.20637) = 5206.37$. Counting 8 remaining (off-by-one) gives 5746.64; the undiscounted $7\times1000$ gives 7000.

questions.q: A 20-year loan of 50000 at 6% annual effective interest is repaid with level annual payments. Calculate the principal repaid in the FIRST payment.
questions.explain: Payment $= 50000/a_{\overline{20}|0.06} = 50000/11.46992 = 4359.23$. First-year interest $= 0.06(50000) = 3000$, so principal $= 4359.23 - 3000 = 1359.23$. The trap answers are the interest portion (3000) and the full payment (4359.23).

concepts.title: The Sinking-Fund Method
concepts.tagline: Pay the lender only interest, and grow the principal separately in a side account. Two interest rates, one clean comparison to amortization.

sections.body: There are two philosophies for killing a loan. **Amortization** blends interest and principal into every payment, whittling the balance to zero. The **sinking-fund method** splits those jobs apart: you pay the lender *interest only* each period — the principal never moves — while quietly feeding a separate side account that grows on its own until, at maturity, it has swollen to exactly the loan amount and extinguishes it in one lump. The exam adores pitting the two against each other, because the comparison turns on a subtle point: the fund usually earns a *different* rate than the loan charges.

sections.title: Interest goes out; savings grow on the side
sections.body: Two money streams run in parallel and you must not let them touch. **Stream one:** you owe the lender interest on the *whole* loan, every single period, $Li$ — and because you never repay principal until the end, that interest charge never shrinks. **Stream two:** you make level deposits $D$ into your own sinking fund, which compounds at *its* rate $j$ (usually lower than the loan rate $i$, because a safe savings vehicle pays less than what you're charged to borrow). The fund climbs until its balance hits $L$, at which instant you hand it to the lender and the debt vanishes. Your true periodic cost is the sum of the two streams: constant interest plus the level deposit.

sections.title: Building the two-stream payment
sections.body: Loan $L$, lender's rate $i$, sinking-fund rate $j$, term $n$. **Interest stream:** principal stays at $L$, so each period you pay $Li$ — flat, forever, until maturity. **Deposit stream:** the deposit $D$ must accumulate to the full loan by time $n$. Since $n$ level deposits at rate $j$ grow to $D\,s_{\overline{n}|j}$, set that equal to $L$ and solve: $$D\,s_{\overline{n}|j} = L \;\Rightarrow\; D = \frac{L}{s_{\overline{n}|j}}.$$ **Total periodic outlay:** $$R = Li + \frac{L}{s_{\overline{n}|j}}.$$ Beautiful fact worth proving to yourself: when the two rates coincide, $i = j$, this *exactly* reproduces the amortization payment $L/a_{\overline{n}|}$. The reason is the identity $\frac{1}{a_{\overline{n}|}} = \frac{1}{s_{\overline{n}|}} + i$ — the level-annuity payment is secretly 'interest plus a sinking-fund deposit' all along. So amortization is just the sinking-fund method with the fund earning the loan rate.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — total payment with two rates
sections.body: A \$10{,}000 loan runs 5 years. The lender charges 8%; your sinking fund earns only 6%. Given $s_{\overline{5}|6\%} = 5.6371$, find the total annual payment, and compare to straight amortization.
steps: **Interest stream:** $10{,}000 \times 0.08 = \$800$ to the lender every year (never changes).

**Compare to amortization at 8%:** $10{,}000/a_{\overline{5}|8\%} = 10{,}000/3.9927 = \$2504.6$ — *cheaper.* The sinking fund costs more here precisely because the fund (6%) earns less than the loan rate (8%); the rate gap is the borrower's penalty.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — net interest in a given year
sections.body: A favorite exam twist: the borrower's *net* cost isn't just $Li$, because the sinking fund is itself earning interest. For the same loan ($D = 1773.96$, $j = 6\%$), find the net interest cost in year 3.
steps: **Fund balance at the start of year 3** (just after the 2nd deposit) $= D\,s_{\overline{2}|6\%} = 1773.96 \times 2.06 = \$3654.4$.
**Interest the fund earns in year 3:** $0.06 \times 3654.4 = \$219.3$ — this offsets your cost.
**Gross interest to the lender:** $Li = \$800$ as always.

**Net interest cost in year 3:** $800 - 219.3 = \$580.7$. As the fund grows, the interest it throws off rises, so your net cost falls year over year — mirroring how amortization's interest portion declines.

sections.title: Net cost = gross interest minus fund earnings
sections.body: To track the 'real' cost in any year, don't just quote $Li$ — subtract what the fund earned: net interest $= Li - j\,(\text{fund balance})$, where the fund balance at time $t$ is $D\,s_{\overline{t}|j}$. This mirrors amortization's shrinking interest column, and it's the lens that makes the $i=j$ equivalence obvious: when the fund earns the loan rate, the net cost schedule *is* the amortization schedule. Memorize the bridge identity $\frac{1}{a_{\overline{n}|}} = \frac{1}{s_{\overline{n}|}} + i$ — it converts between the two worlds in one line.

sections.title: Two rates, and a principal that never moves
sections.body: The whole concept hinges on keeping **two rates** straight: $i$ is charged by the lender (drives the interest payment $Li$), while $j$ is earned by you (drives the accumulation $s_{\overline{n}|j}$). Swap them — put the loan rate inside the $s$ factor, or accumulate at the loan rate — and the answer collapses. Second trap: the outstanding *principal* under a sinking fund does **not** amortize down; it sits at $L$ the entire term, so the interest payment is a flat $Li$ every period, never declining. (What declines is the *net* cost, via fund earnings — a different quantity.)

cards.front: Why does the sinking-fund total equal the amortization payment when $i=j$?
cards.back: Because of the identity $\frac{1}{a_{\overline{n}|}} = \frac{1}{s_{\overline{n}|}} + i$: the amortization payment $L/a_{\overline{n}|}$ is literally interest $Li$ plus a sinking-fund deposit $L/s_{\overline{n}|}$ when both use the same rate.

cards.front: Under a sinking fund, what stays constant and what changes year to year?
cards.back: The principal ($L$) and gross interest to the lender ($Li$) stay flat the whole term; the fund balance grows, so the *net* interest cost $Li - j(\text{fund balance})$ falls each year.

questions.q: A \$5000 loan at 10% uses a sinking fund earning 8%, 4 years, $s_{\overline{4}|8\%}=4.5061$. Find the annual sinking-fund deposit.
Same loan: \$5000 at 10% lender rate. What is the annual interest paid to the lender?
questions.explain: Interest only on the full principal: $5000(0.10)=500$, every year.

questions.q: Combine the two: total annual payment for the \$5000 loan (interest \$500, deposit \$1109.61)?
Under the sinking-fund method, the outstanding loan principal over time:
questions.explain: Only interest is paid to the lender; principal is retired in a lump at maturity, so it stays at $L$ throughout.

questions.q: The sinking-fund total payment equals the amortization payment exactly when:
questions.explain: With equal rates, $Li + L/s_{\overline{n}|} = L/a_{\overline{n}|}$, reproducing amortization.

questions.q: A loan of 10000 is repaid by the sinking fund method over 10 years. The lender charges 8% annual effective interest on the loan; the sinking fund earns 6% annual effective. Calculate the total annual payment (interest plus sinking-fund deposit).
questions.explain: Interest to the lender each year $= 0.08(10000) = 800$. Sinking-fund deposit to accumulate 10000 in 10 years at 6% $= 10000/s_{\overline{10}|0.06} = 10000/13.18080 = 758.68$. Total $= 800 + 758.68 = 1558.68$. The deposit alone (758.68) and the equivalent amortization payment at 8% (1490.29) are the traps.

questions.q: A borrower repays a 10000 loan by the sinking fund method over 5 years, paying 8% interest annually to the lender and depositing into a fund earning 5% to rebuild the principal. Calculate the annual sinking-fund deposit.
questions.explain: Deposit $= 10000/s_{\overline{5}|0.05} = 10000/5.525631 = 1809.75$. Dividing principal by 5 with no interest gives 2000; adding the 800 interest payment gives the total cost 2609.75, not the deposit.

modules.title: Bonds
modules.blurb: Pricing coupon bonds, the premium/discount relationship to the yield, and book value via amortization of the bond's premium or discount.

concepts.title: Bond Pricing & Premium/Discount
concepts.tagline: A bond is an annuity of coupons plus a lump-sum redemption. Whether it trades above or below par is decided by one comparison.

sections.body: A bond intimidates beginners and then turns out to be two old friends stapled together: a stream of equal coupons (a level **annuity**) plus one big redemption payment at the end (a single **discounted lump sum**). You already price both. Add them and you've priced the bond. The only genuinely new idea is *premium vs discount* — whether the bond costs more or less than it pays back — and that's settled by one ten-second glance at coupon-rate-versus-yield, before you touch the calculator.

sections.title: Why a generous coupon forces the price above par
sections.body: Think like a buyer. A bond's coupon rate is fixed at issue, but the market's required yield drifts. Suppose a bond pays an 8% coupon while the market only demands 6%. That coupon is *too good* — everyone wants it — so buyers bid the price *up* until the richer coupon, spread over a higher purchase price, nets out to just the 6% the market requires. The bond sells at a **premium** (above redemption value). Flip it: a coupon stingier than the market yield can't attract buyers at face value, so the price sinks to a **discount** until the bargain price compensates for the weak coupon. Coupon exactly equal to yield → no adjustment needed → it sells at **par**. So before any arithmetic, the comparison *coupon rate vs yield* already tells you which side of par the price lands on.

sections.title: Assembling the price from its two pieces
sections.body:
Don't memorize the bond formula as a monolith — build it. **Piece 1, the coupons:** each period the bond pays $Fr$ (face $F$ times coupon rate $r$), for $n$ periods. That's a level annuity worth $Fr\,a_{\overline{n}|}$ at the yield $i$. **Piece 2, the redemption:** a single payment $C$ (usually $= F$) arriving at time $n$, worth $Cv^n$ today. Add them: $$P = Fr\,a_{\overline{n}|} + C v^n.$$ Everything discounts at the **yield** $i$ — that's the rate the market demands, living inside both $a_{\overline{n}|}$ and $v^n$.

**The premium/discount formula** makes the intuition exact. Substitute $a_{\overline{n}|} = \frac{1-v^n}{i}$ and simplify (take $C=F$): $$P = C + (Fr - Ci)\,a_{\overline{n}|}.$$ Read it directly: the price is redemption value $C$ *plus* the present value of the per-period 'coupon excess' $(Fr - Ci)$. If the coupon $Fr$ beats the yield-on-redemption $Ci$, that term is positive — a **premium**. If it's negative — a **discount**. The sign of $(Fr - Ci)$ *is* the premium/discount, proven.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — price a 10-year coupon bond
sections.body: A \$1000 par bond pays 8% annual coupons, redeems at par in 10 years, and is priced to yield 6%. Find the price two ways.
steps: **Predict first:** coupon 8% > yield 6% → premium → expect $P > 1000$ before computing.

**Cross-check with the premium formula:** $P = C + (Fr - Ci)a_{\overline{n}|} = 1000 + (80 - 60)(7.3601) = 1000 + 147.20 = \$1147.20$. The \$147.20 premium is exactly the PV of the \$20/yr coupon excess — matching, and $P>1000$ as predicted.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — a semiannual bond (period discipline)
sections.body: The exam's favorite bond is semiannual. A \$1000 bond pays 7% coupons *convertible semiannually*, redeems at par in 5 years, yielding 8% convertible semiannually. Price it — the whole challenge is halving and doubling consistently.
steps: **Convert everything to half-year units:** coupon per period $= \frac{0.07}{2}\times 1000 = \$35$; yield per period $= \frac{0.08}{2} = 4\%$; number of periods $n = 5\times 2 = 10$ half-years.
**Sanity:** coupon 7% < yield 8% → discount → $P < 1000$. Confirmed.

sections.title: Call premium/discount before you compute
sections.body: Always glance at coupon-rate vs yield first and write down 'premium' or 'discount' before pricing. Coupon > yield → premium → the price *must* exceed redemption; coupon < yield → discount → below redemption. This does two things: it eliminates wrong multiple-choice options at a glance, and it catches keystroke errors instantly — if you predicted premium but your calculator says \$940, you fat-fingered a rate. The prediction costs five seconds and saves the whole question.

sections.title: Semiannual everything — halve and double in lockstep
sections.body: The signature bond mistake is a period mismatch. Most bonds pay **semiannually**, so *three* things must switch to half-year units together: the coupon becomes $Fr/2$, the yield becomes the per-half-year rate ($i^{(2)}/2$), and $n$ becomes the number of half-years (years $\times 2$). Halve the coupon and yield but forget to double $n$ — or discount semiannual coupons at an annual yield — and the price is garbage. Decide 'this whole problem lives in half-years' up front and convert all three quantities at once, before any factor is computed.

cards.front: What are the two pieces of a bond price, and at what rate do they discount?
cards.back: Coupons as a level annuity $Fr\,a_{\overline{n}|}$ plus the redemption $Cv^n$, both discounted at the market *yield* $i$ — not the coupon rate.

cards.front: Prove which way a bond trades from $P = C + (Fr-Ci)a_{\overline{n}|}$.
cards.back: The price is redemption plus the PV of the coupon excess $(Fr-Ci)$: positive → premium ($P>C$), negative → discount ($P<C$), zero → par. The sign of $Fr-Ci$ decides it.

questions.q: A \$1000 par bond with 5% annual coupons redeems at par in 8 years, priced to yield 5%. Its price is:
questions.explain: Coupon rate equals yield (5% = 5%), so the bond is priced exactly at par: \$1000.

questions.q: A bond with a coupon rate below its yield rate will be priced:
questions.explain: Coupon < yield means the coupons are unattractive, so the price falls below redemption — a discount bond.

questions.q: A \$1000 par, 6% annual-coupon bond redeems at par in 5 years, yielding 8%. Find the price. ($a_{\overline{5}|}=3.9927$ at 8%, $v^5=0.68058$)
A \$1000 par bond pays 7% annual coupons, redeems at \$1050 in 10 years, and yields 7%. The price is:
questions.explain: Coupon is $1000(0.07)=70$ on a $1050$ redemption. The price $P = 70a_{\overline{10}|} + 1050v^{10}$ at 7% comes out between 1000 and 1050 because redemption exceeds face. (It equals about \$1025.)

questions.q: A semiannual bond has 6% annual coupons (paid twice yearly), \$1000 par, 3 years to maturity, yielding 8% annual convertible semiannually. How many periods and what coupon per period?
questions.explain: Semiannual: $n = 3\times2 = 6$ periods, coupon $= 1000(0.06)/2 = 30$ per period, yield $= 8\%/2 = 4\%$ per period.

questions.q: A 1000 par-value bond with 8% annual coupons matures in 10 years, redeemable at par. Calculate its price to yield 6% annual effective.
questions.explain: Price $= Fr\,a_{\overline{10}|0.06} + C v^{10} = 80(7.360087) + 1000(0.558395) = 588.81 + 558.40 = 1147.20$. Since the 8% coupon exceeds the 6% yield, the bond sells at a premium (above the 1000 par).

questions.q: A 1000 par-value bond pays 6% annual coupons semiannually (30 per half-year) and matures in 10 years at par. Calculate its price to yield 8% convertible semiannually.
questions.explain: Work in half-years: $n = 20$, coupon $= 30$, yield $= 4\%$ per period. Price $= 30\,a_{\overline{20}|0.04} + 1000 v^{20} = 30(13.590326) + 1000(0.456387) = 407.71 + 456.39 = 864.10$. The coupon (6%) below the yield (8%) makes it a discount bond (below par).

concepts.title: Bond Amortization & Book Value
concepts.tagline: Between purchase and maturity a bond's book value glides to par. Each coupon splits into interest earned and a write-down (or write-up) of premium or discount.

sections.body: Here's a small paradox that this concept resolves. You pay \$1075 for a bond that will redeem for only \$1000 — and yet it's a perfectly fair deal earning your required yield. How? Over the bond's life its book value must *glide down* from \$1075 to \$1000, and each fat coupon quietly hands back a piece of your overpayment along the way. That glide is **amortization of premium** (downhill) or **accretion of discount** (uphill), and the engine behind it is one idea you already met in loan amortization: every payment is *interest plus a correction.*

sections.title: Each coupon = interest earned + a book-value correction
sections.body:
Stop thinking of the coupon as pure income. Each period the bond genuinely *earns* the yield on whatever it's currently worth: interest $= i \times BV$. The coupon you actually pocket is fixed at $Fr$, and it rarely equals that earned interest — so the difference has to go somewhere, and where it goes is the book value.

**Premium bond** (fat coupon, $Fr >$ earned interest): you're collecting more than you truly earned, so the surplus is really a *return of your overpayment* — it writes the book value **down** toward par. **Discount bond** (skinny coupon, $Fr <$ earned interest): you're collecting less than you earned, and the shortfall is paid by the bond becoming worth **more** — the book value is written **up** toward par.
