Either direction, the book value is *pulled to par by maturity*, because at redemption it must equal $C$. This is the loan-amortization split (interest vs principal) wearing a bond costume.

sections.title: Book value and the write-down, derived
sections.body:
**Book value** is just the bond re-priced at the *original* yield using only the cash flows that remain: $$BV_t = Fr\,a_{\overline{n-t}|i} + C\,v^{n-t}.$$ It's the same two-piece price formula, with the clock advanced. **The split of coupon $t$:** interest earned $= i\,BV_{t-1}$; book-value adjustment $= Fr - i\,BV_{t-1}$ (positive write-down for a premium, negative — i.e. a write-up — for a discount).

**Why the adjustments grow by $(1+i)$.** Let the period-$t$ write-down be $w_t = Fr - iBV_{t-1}$. The book value moves by exactly that write-down: $BV_t = BV_{t-1} - w_t$. Then $w_{t+1} - w_t = -i(BV_t - BV_{t-1}) = -i(-w_t) = iw_t$, so $$w_{t+1} = (1+i)w_t.$$ Identical algebra to the loan-principal ladder — the write-downs (or write-ups) form a geometric sequence with ratio $(1+i)$. So the $k$-th adjustment is $w_1(1+i)^{k-1}$, and you can leap to any year without building the table.

widget.caption: Set the coupon rate against the yield and watch the book value glide to par: above-yield coupons make a **premium** bond amortize *downward*, below-yield coupons make a **discount** bond accrete *upward*. The write-down/write-up each period is exactly the gap between the coupon and the interest earned on the current book value.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — one line of the schedule
sections.body: A \$1000 par bond with 8% annual coupons yields 6%, redeems at par. Its current book value is \$1075. Find this period's interest earned, the premium amortized, and the new book value.
steps: **Coupon received:** $Fr = 1000(0.08) = 80$ (fixed).
**Interest actually earned:** yield times *current book value*, $0.06(1075) = \$64.50$.
**Premium amortized (write-down):** the surplus coupon, $80 - 64.50 = \$15.50$.
**New book value:** $1075 - 15.50 = \$1059.50$ — nudged toward par, exactly as a premium bond must move.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — jump to a future year with the ladder
sections.body: For the same bond, suppose the *first* premium amortized (in year 1) is \$14.61. Without building the whole schedule, find the premium amortized in year 5 and the total amortized over years 1–5.
steps: **Use the geometric ladder** $w_k = w_1(1+i)^{k-1}$ with $w_1 = 14.61$, $i = 6\%$.
**Total over years 1–5** is a geometric sum: $w_1\,s_{\overline{5}|6\%}$... more directly, $14.61\cdot\dfrac{(1.06)^5 - 1}{0.06} = 14.61(5.6371) = \$82.36$.
**Interpretation:** the book value fell \$82.36 over those five years — and you never touched a coupon-by-coupon table. The ladder turns a schedule grind into one multiplication.

widget.caption: Set the coupon rate against the yield and watch the book value glide to par: above-yield coupons make a **premium** bond amortize *downward*, below-yield coupons make a **discount** bond accrete *upward*. The write-down/write-up each period is exactly the gap between the coupon and the interest earned on the current book value.

sections.title: Interest is yield × book value — never coupon, never par
sections.body: The earned interest each period is $i \times BV_{t-1}$: the **yield** times the **current book value**. Three ways students get this wrong: using the coupon as the interest (the coupon is cash received, not interest earned), using the yield times *par* (only equals book value at par), or using the *coupon rate* instead of the yield. Each only coincidentally matches at par, which is exactly why par problems lull you into the bad habit. Second trap: signs — a premium writes **down**, a discount writes **up**; invert that and your whole schedule drifts the wrong way and misses par at maturity.

cards.front: Why does each coupon split into 'interest earned' and a book-value adjustment, and what's the interest piece?
cards.back: The bond earns $i\times BV_{t-1}$ (yield on current value); the coupon $Fr$ differs from that, and the gap adjusts book value — down for a premium, up for a discount. Same idea as loan I/P split.

cards.front: Prove the premium-amortized amounts grow by $(1+i)$.
cards.back: With $w_t = Fr - iBV_{t-1}$ and $BV_t = BV_{t-1}-w_t$: $w_{t+1}-w_t = -i(BV_t-BV_{t-1}) = iw_t$, so $w_{t+1}=(1+i)w_t$ — a geometric ladder, $w_k=w_1(1+i)^{k-1}$.

questions.q: A bond with book value \$980 yields 7% and pays a \$50 coupon. Find the interest earned this period.
Same bond (BV \$980, yield 7%, coupon \$50). Is it a discount or premium bond, and what is the book-value adjustment?
questions.explain: Coupon 50 < interest earned 68.60, so the shortfall \$18.60 writes the book value UP — a discount bond accreting toward par.

questions.q: A premium bond's first-year premium amortized is \$12 at yield 5%. What is the second-year amount?
questions.explain: Amortization grows by $(1+i)$: $12(1.05)=12.60$.

questions.q: If a bond is priced at par, the book-value amortization each period is:
questions.explain: At par the coupon exactly equals the interest earned, so there is no write-up or write-down: book value stays at par.

questions.q: A \$1000 bond redeems at par with book value \$1038.10 one year before maturity, yield 5%, coupon \$90. Find the final book value at maturity.
questions.explain: Interest $=0.05(1038.10)=51.90$; amortized $=90-51.90=38.10$; $BV=1038.10-38.10=1000.00$ — exactly the par redemption value.

questions.q: A 1000 par bond with 9% annual coupons, redeemable at par in 5 years, is bought to yield 7% annual effective. Calculate the premium amortized (write-down of book value) in the first coupon.
questions.explain: Price (book value) $= 90\,a_{\overline{5}|0.07} + 1000 v^5 = 369.02 + 712.99 = 1082.00$. First-coupon interest earned $= 0.07(1082.00) = 75.74$; the write-down $= $ coupon $-$ interest $= 90 - 75.74 = 14.26$. The trap answers are the full coupon (90) and the interest portion (75.74).

questions.q: A bond bought at a premium has a book value of 1050 just after a coupon. It yields 4% per period and pays a coupon of 60 each period. Calculate the book value immediately after the NEXT coupon.
questions.explain: Book value rolls forward at the yield, then the coupon is paid: $B_{k+1} = B_k(1+i) - \text{coupon} = 1050(1.04) - 60 = 1092 - 60 = 1032$. Forgetting to subtract the coupon leaves 1092; a premium bond's book value should fall toward redemption, which 1032 does.

concepts.title: Callable Bonds & Yield to Worst
concepts.tagline: When the issuer can redeem early, price the bond as if the worst call date for you is certain. One rule picks the date.

sections.body: A **callable** bond comes with a catch buried in the fine print: the *issuer* can hand you your money back early and stop paying coupons — and they'll do it precisely when it's good for them, which is precisely when it's bad for you. You're selling them an option, and you must price the bond as if they'll exercise it at the worst possible moment for you. The entire skill is figuring out *which* redemption date is the worst — and there's a one-line rule that beats testing them all.

sections.title: The issuer calls when it's cheap for them — so plan for your worst case
sections.body: Why would an issuer redeem early? When rates have fallen and they can refinance their debt more cheaply — they'd rather pay off your fat old bond and reissue at today's lower rates. That decision is made in *their* interest, never yours. So as the buyer you can't assume the rosy scenario; you must assume the issuer picks the redemption date that gives *you* the **lowest** value. Concretely: compute the price at every allowable call date and **take the minimum** — the famous 'yield to worst.' Pay any more than that minimum and, if the bond is called at the bad-for-you date, you've locked in a yield below what you wanted. The minimum price is your safe maximum bid.

sections.title: Why premium calls early and discount calls late — derived
sections.body:
The brute-force method: price the bond at each candidate redemption date and take the smallest. But you can usually *predict* the worst date with one observation. Recall the premium/discount formula $P = C + (Fr - Ci)\,a_{\overline{n}|}$.

**Premium bond** ($Fr > Ci$): the coupon-excess term $(Fr-Ci)a_{\overline{n}|}$ is *positive* and *grows with $n$* (longer annuity → bigger $a_{\overline{n}|}$). So a *longer* life means a *higher* price — which means the **shortest** life gives the **lowest** price. Worst-for-you = **earliest** call date. (Intuitively: a premium bond's value is its above-market coupons; the sooner it's called, the fewer of those golden coupons you collect.)

**Discount bond** ($Fr < Ci$): now $(Fr-Ci)$ is *negative*, so a longer annuity makes the price *lower* — the **longest** life gives the minimum. Worst-for-you = **latest** date (maturity). So the rule isn't memorization, it's the sign of $(Fr-Ci)$ telling you which direction stretches the price down.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — which date to price (premium)
sections.body: A \$1000 bond pays 9% annual coupons and is callable at par at the end of years 8, 9, or 10. You want a 7% yield. Which date do you price for, and why?
steps: **Premium or discount?** Coupon 9% > yield 7% → premium at every date.
**Direction of price vs life:** for a premium bond, $(Fr-Ci) = (90-70) = 20 > 0$, so price *rises* with more remaining years.
**Therefore the minimum price is at the shortest life** — the **earliest** call, end of year 8. Price it as an 8-year bond.
**Why it matters:** if you naively priced for year 10 you'd pay more, and a year-8 call would crater your realized yield below 7%.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — when a call premium breaks the rule
sections.body: A \$1000, 6%-annual-coupon bond yields 7% and is callable at \$1050 at end of year 5 or at par (\$1000) at maturity, year 10. The shortcut says 'discount → latest,' but the varying redemption value means you must check. Show the safe approach.
steps: **The clean rule assumes a constant redemption value** — here $C$ is \$1050 at year 5 but \$1000 at year 10, so the sign-of-$(Fr-Ci)$ shortcut is no longer reliable. Price both dates explicitly.
**Take the minimum:** \$929.77 (year 10). Pay no more — the extra call premium at year 5 wasn't enough to make the early date the worst here.

sections.title: Premium → earliest, discount → latest (par calls only)
sections.body: When every call is at the *same* redemption value (usually par), skip the computation marathon: **premium bonds are priced for the earliest call, discount bonds for the latest.** A premium bond's worth is its surplus coupons, so the issuer yanks it as soon as allowed — earliest. A discount bond climbs toward par, so the issuer gains nothing by calling early — latest. One glance at coupon-vs-yield picks the date. But the instant the redemption value *varies* by date (a call premium), this one-liner can lie — fall back to pricing each date and taking the minimum.

sections.title: Call premiums void the shortcut; always frame as minimum price
sections.body: Two things sink students. **(1) Varying redemption values:** if the bond can be called *above* par with the premium shrinking over time, the redemption $C$ changes by date and the tidy premium→early / discount→late rule no longer holds — you must price each candidate date and compare, as in Worked Example 2. **(2) Logic inversion under pressure:** always operationalize it as 'the **minimum price** over all dates,' not a fuzzy 'best for the issuer.' They coincide, but the minimum-price framing is concrete and keeps you from flipping the comparison when the clock is ticking.

cards.front: Why is a callable bond priced at the *minimum* over redemption dates?
cards.back: The issuer calls in their own interest (when rates fall), i.e. the date worst for you. As a buyer you must survive that, so your safe price is the lowest across all allowable dates — 'yield to worst.'

cards.front: Derive which call date is worst for a par-redemption premium bond.
cards.back: Price $= C + (Fr-Ci)a_{\overline{n}|}$ with $Fr>Ci$, so price rises with $n$; the minimum is at the shortest life → earliest call. (Discount: $Fr<Ci$ → price falls with $n$ → latest. Breaks if $C$ varies by date.)

questions.q: A bond with coupon rate above its yield (a premium bond) callable at par should be priced assuming a call at the:
questions.explain: Premium bonds lose value toward par, so the issuer calls as early as allowed; price for the earliest call.

questions.q: A discount bond (coupon below yield) callable at par should be priced assuming redemption at the:
questions.explain: A discount bond gains value toward par; the issuer won't call early, so use the latest date.

questions.q: The price you should pay for a callable bond is the ____ across all redemption dates.
questions.explain: To be safe against the issuer's worst-for-you choice, pay the minimum price (yield to worst).

questions.q: Why does an issuer call a bond when interest rates fall?
choices: To refinance at a lower rate
questions.explain: Lower market rates let the issuer reissue debt more cheaply, so calling and refinancing benefits them.

questions.q: A bond is callable at par at years 5–10 and is priced to yield less than its coupon. The investor should assume a call at year:
questions.explain: Coupon > yield means a premium bond → called at the earliest date, year 5.

questions.q: A 1000 par bond with 10% annual coupons is callable at par at the end of year 8, 9, or 10. An investor wants a yield of at least 8% annual effective. Calculate the maximum price the investor should pay (price to worst).
questions.explain: The 10% coupon exceeds the 8% yield, so it's a premium bond — the worst (lowest-price) outcome is the EARLIEST call, year 8: $100\,a_{\overline{8}|0.08} + 1000 v^8 = 574.66 + 540.27 = 1114.93$. Calling at year 9 or 10 gives higher prices (1124.94, 1134.20); paying those risks falling short of 8% if called early.

questions.q: A 1000 par bond with 6% annual coupons, redeemable at par, is callable at the end of year 5 or held to maturity at the end of year 10. An investor requires a 7% annual effective yield. Calculate the price to worst.
questions.explain: The 6% coupon is below the 7% yield, so it's a discount bond — the worst (lowest-price) outcome is the LATEST redemption, year 10: $60\,a_{\overline{10}|0.07} + 1000 v^{10} = 421.41 + 508.35 = 929.76$. The year-5 call gives a higher 959.00; pricing at the lower 929.76 guarantees at least 7% either way.

concepts.title: Yield Rates, NPV & IRR
concepts.tagline: The yield rate is the discount rate that makes a project break even. NPV ranks projects; IRR is the rate where NPV hits zero.

sections.body: Strip every capital-budgeting decision down and you find two questions. **Net present value** asks: *at the rate I demand, does this project add value or destroy it?* **Internal rate of return** asks: *what rate would make this project exactly break even?* They're two views of the same NPV curve — one reads off the height at your hurdle rate, the other reads off where the curve crosses zero. Master that picture and you'll also see *why* IRR misbehaves on certain cash flows, which is precisely where the exam lays its traps.

sections.title: NPV is value created; IRR is where that value hits zero
sections.body:
Picture NPV as a function of the discount rate. Sign every cash flow (money out negative, money in positive), discount each back to today, and add: that's $\text{NPV}(i)$. At a low rate, future inflows are barely discounted, so a good project's NPV is high and positive. Crank the rate up and those inflows shrink, dragging NPV down. Somewhere it crosses zero — *that crossing rate is the IRR*, the project's own internal earning rate.

So the two tools are the same curve: **NPV at your required rate** tells you the dollar value created (positive → accept); the **IRR** is the rate where that value vanishes. Comparing IRR to your hurdle is just asking 'are we to the left of the crossing?' — if IRR > hurdle, NPV at the hurdle is still positive.

sections.title: NPV, the IRR condition, and why IRR can break
sections.body:
**NPV** at rate $i$: $$\text{NPV}(i) = \sum_{t} \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t}.$$ Accept a standalone project when $\text{NPV} > 0$ at the required rate. **IRR** is the rate $i^*$ that zeroes it: $$\text{NPV}(i^*) = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+i^*)^t} = 0.$$

Why can IRR misbehave? Substitute $x = \frac{1}{1+i}$ and the NPV becomes a *polynomial* in $x$: $\sum_t CF_t\,x^t$. A polynomial can have several positive real roots — and by **Descartes' rule of signs**, the number of positive IRRs is at most the number of times the cash-flow sequence *changes sign*. One sign change (the normal 'pay once, receive thereafter' project) → exactly one IRR, clean. Two sign changes (pay, receive, pay again) → possibly two IRRs or none, and the single-rate story collapses. This is not a quirk to memorize — it's just what polynomials do.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — NPV decision and locating the IRR
sections.body: A project costs \$1000 now and returns \$600 at year 1 and \$600 at year 2. At a required rate of 10%, find the NPV, decide, and bracket the IRR.
steps: **Net against the cost:** NPV $= 1041.32 - 1000 = +\$41.32$ → positive → **accept**.
**What does that imply about IRR?** NPV is positive at 10%, so the zero-crossing lies *above* 10%.

**Pin it down:** set $-1000 + 600x + 600x^2 = 0$ with $x = 1/(1+i)$. Solving the quadratic, $x = 0.8844$, so $i^* = 1/0.8844 - 1 = 13.07\%$ — comfortably above the 10% hurdle, consistent with NPV > 0.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — the NPV-vs-IRR conflict on scale
sections.body: Two *mutually exclusive* projects at a 10% cost of capital. A: invest \$100, get \$150 in one year. B: invest \$1000, get \$1300 in one year. Show why IRR and NPV disagree and which wins.
steps: **IRRs:** A breaks even at $150/100 - 1 = 50\%$; B at $1300/1000 - 1 = 30\%$. By IRR, A looks better.
**The conflict:** A has the higher *rate* but B creates five times the *value*. IRR ignores scale — a fabulous return on a tiny base.
**Resolution:** for mutually exclusive choices, pick the higher **NPV** → choose B. You can't deposit a percentage in the bank; you deposit dollars, and B delivers \$181.8 of them.
sections.answer: Choose B (higher NPV \$181.8), despite A's higher IRR

sections.title: Rank by NPV; reach for IRR only for a break-even rate
sections.body: When projects compete for the same dollar (mutually exclusive), rank by **NPV at the cost of capital** — full stop. IRR ignores scale (Worked Example 2), and when cash-flow signs flip more than once it can spit out multiple roots or none. NPV always returns one clean, value-denominated answer. Use IRR when the question genuinely asks 'what single rate does this earn?' or to compare against a hurdle for a *standalone* accept/reject — not to rank alternatives.

sections.title: Multiple IRRs and the reinvestment fantasy
sections.body: Two classic snares. **(1) Multiple/no IRR:** if the signs change more than once (out, in, out), Descartes warns of up to that many IRRs — quoting 'the' IRR is meaningless; fall back to NPV. **(2) The reinvestment assumption:** IRR implicitly assumes every interim cash flow is *reinvested at the IRR itself*. A project boasting a 40% IRR is only worth 40% if you can actually redeploy its cash at 40% — usually you can't. NPV makes the honest assumption (reinvest at the cost of capital), which is another reason it's the trustworthy ranking tool.

cards.front: How are NPV and IRR two readings of the same curve?
cards.back: NPV($i$) is a downward-sloping curve in the rate; its height at your hurdle rate is the value created, and the rate where it crosses zero is the IRR. NPV>0 at the hurdle ⟺ IRR>hurdle.

cards.front: Why can a cash-flow stream have multiple IRRs?
cards.back: NPV is a polynomial in $x=1/(1+i)$; by Descartes' rule the number of positive roots is bounded by the number of sign changes in the cash flows. More than one sign change → possibly multiple IRRs.

questions.q: A project costs \$500 and returns \$300 at year 1 and \$300 at year 2. At 8%, find the NPV.
The internal rate of return is defined as the rate at which:
questions.explain: IRR is the discount rate making the net present value exactly zero.

questions.q: A project has NPV $> 0$ at your required rate. This means the IRR is:
questions.explain: If NPV is positive at the hurdle rate, the break-even rate (IRR) lies above it.

questions.q: Cash flows are $-100, +260, -165$. Descartes' rule of signs suggests up to how many positive IRRs?
questions.explain: Two sign changes ($-$ to $+$ to $-$) allow up to two positive real IRRs.

questions.q: For ranking two mutually exclusive projects, the preferred criterion is:
choices: Higher NPV at the cost of capital
questions.explain: NPV at the cost of capital ranks by value created and avoids IRR's scale and multiple-root issues.

concepts.title: Dollar-Weighted vs Time-Weighted Yield
concepts.tagline: Two ways to measure a fund's return. One judges the timing of deposits; the other judges the manager. The exam wants both.

sections.body: A fund posts a return — but *whose* return is it really? Suppose a client dumped in a big deposit right before a roaring quarter. Did the *manager* suddenly get good, or did the *client* just get lucky with timing? These are different questions, and they need different yardsticks. **Dollar-weighted** yield credits (or blames) the timing and size of cash flows — it grades the investor. **Time-weighted** yield surgically removes timing to expose the manager's raw skill. Knowing which is which, and *why* they diverge, is a near-guaranteed exam question.

sections.title: One measures the investor's timing, the other the manager's skill
sections.body:
**Dollar-weighted** return is nothing more than the **IRR of the fund's actual cash flows.** Because IRR weights each period by how many dollars were present, a fat deposit sitting through a good stretch *inflates* the figure — and a deposit before a bad stretch drags it down. So dollar-weighting answers 'how did the *money* do,' which is really a verdict on the *investor's timing decisions.*

**Time-weighted** return refuses to let deposits matter. It chops the year into sub-periods at each cash-flow date, measures the pure growth factor *within* each sub-period (where the dollar amount is fixed), and chains those factors together. A deposit changes the base going into the next sub-period but never counts as 'performance.' The result is the return on a single dollar left untouched all year — a clean grade for the *manager.*

sections.title: Building both yields from the equation of value
sections.body:
**Dollar-weighted = IRR.** Write the fund's equation of value over the year: start balance $A$ grows, deposits/withdrawals $C_t$ are accumulated to year-end, and it must reconcile to the end balance $B$: $$A(1+i) + \sum_t C_t (1+i)^{1-t} = B.$$ Solve for $i$ — that's the dollar-weighted yield. When the exam wants speed, use the simple-interest approximation (deposits earn interest only for the fraction of the year they're present): $$i \approx \frac{I}{A + \sum_t C_t(1-t)},$$ where $I$ is total interest earned and $t$ is the fraction of the year *elapsed* before deposit $C_t$.

**Time-weighted = chained growth.** Split at every cash flow and multiply the sub-period factors: $$1 + i_{tw} = \prod_k \frac{B_k^{-}}{B_{k-1}^{+}},$$ each factor being the balance *just before* the next cash flow over the balance *just after* the previous one. The deposits live in the denominators as new bases, never in the numerators as gains.

sections.title: Worked example 1 — time-weighted with a mid-year deposit
sections.body: A fund starts at \$100. After 6 months it is worth \$110; you then deposit \$50 (balance jumps to \$160). At year-end it is worth \$180. Find the time-weighted yield.
steps: **Sub-period 1 (before the deposit):** growth factor $= 110/100 = 1.10$.
**Sub-period 2 (after the deposit):** growth factor $= 180/160 = 1.125$. The \$50 deposit raised the *base* to 160 — it is *not* counted as a gain, which is why we divide by 160, not 110.
**Chain the factors:** $1 + i_{tw} = 1.10 \times 1.125 = 1.2375$.
**Time-weighted yield** $= 23.75\%$ — the manager's per-dollar performance, untouched by the deposit's timing.

sections.title: Worked example 2 — dollar-weighted on the same fund
sections.body: Same fund (\$100 start, \$50 deposited at mid-year, \$180 end). Compute the dollar-weighted yield with the simple-interest approximation and compare it to the 23.75% time-weighted figure.
steps: **Total interest earned:** end minus start minus net deposits $= 180 - 100 - 50 = \$30$.
**Exposure base:** the \$100 is present all year; the \$50 deposit is present only the second half ($1-t = 0.5$). Base $= 100 + 50(0.5) = 125$.
**Approximate dollar-weighted yield:** $i \approx \dfrac{30}{125} = 0.24 = 24.0\%$.

**Compare:** dollar-weighted (24.0%) slightly exceeds time-weighted (23.75%). The deposit landed *before* the strong second half, so extra dollars were present for the gain — the investor's timing helped, and only the dollar-weighted figure rewards it.

sections.title: Compare the two to grade the investor's timing
sections.body: The *gap* between the yields is itself the answer to 'did the client's timing help?' If big deposits arrived just **before** strong performance, dollar-weighted > time-weighted (more money enjoyed the gain). If money arrived before a **weak** stretch, dollar-weighted < time-weighted. Time-weighted is deliberately blind to all of it. So a quick sanity move on any problem: predict the *sign* of (dollar-weighted − time-weighted) from when the cash flows landed relative to the good/bad periods — if your computed numbers contradict that prediction, recheck.

sections.title: Don't let deposits inflate the time-weighted return
sections.body: The signature error: counting a deposit as investment *gain*. In the worked example, the balance jumped from 110 to 160, but \$50 of that was new money — the performance factor uses $180/160$, not $180/110$. Time-weighting deliberately quarantines cash flows at sub-period boundaries. For dollar-weighting, remember it is an IRR, so a withdrawal is a *negative* cash flow in the equation of value.

cards.front: Why does the time-weighted return divide by the post-deposit balance (180/160), never 180/110?
cards.back: Because a deposit is new money, not investment gain. Time-weighting splits the year at each cash flow and resets the base to the post-deposit balance, so the growth factor measures only what the manager earned on the dollars actually invested.

cards.front: Two funds report identical time-weighted returns but different dollar-weighted returns. What does that tell you?
cards.back: The manager performed equally well in both; the investors timed their deposits differently. The higher dollar-weighted figure belongs to the fund whose large contributions happened to land just before the strong stretch — that is investor timing, not manager skill.

questions.q: A fund grows \$100 → \$120 in H1, takes a \$30 deposit (to \$150), then ends H2 at \$165. Find the time-weighted yield.
The dollar-weighted yield is computed as the:
questions.explain: Dollar-weighted return is the internal rate of return solving the fund's equation of value.

questions.q: An investor adds a large sum just before a strong period. Compared to time-weighted, the dollar-weighted return is:
questions.explain: More dollars present during the gain raises the dollar-weighted (IRR) return above the time-weighted figure.

questions.q: Which return best isolates an investment manager's skill, independent of client deposits?
questions.explain: Time-weighting removes the effect of cash-flow timing, leaving the manager's per-dollar performance.

questions.q: Fund: \$1000 start, \$80 interest earned over the year, a \$200 deposit at mid-year. Approximate the dollar-weighted yield via $I/(A+C(1-t))$.

concepts.title: Spot Rates & Forward Rates
concepts.tagline: The yield curve is not one rate but a term structure. Spot rates price each maturity; forward rates are the future rates locked in today.

sections.body: A single interest rate is a convenient fiction. In reality, money for 1 year and money for 5 years command *different* rates — the **term structure**. **Spot rates** are today's rate for each maturity; **forward rates** are the rates for future periods that today's curve implicitly locks in. Reading one off the other is a high-frequency FM skill, and it powers swaps and bond pricing alike.

sections.title: No-arbitrage links the long path to the short paths
sections.body: Investing for 2 years at the 2-year spot rate must give the *same* growth as investing 1 year at the 1-year spot and then rolling into a rate locked in today for year 2 — otherwise a riskless profit exists. That locked-in second-year rate is the **forward rate**. So the long spot rate is a geometric blend of the short spot and the forwards: the multi-year accumulation factors must agree no matter how you slice the path.

sections.title: Spot–forward relationship
sections.body: Let $s_t$ be the $t$-year spot rate and $f_{[t-1,t]}$ the 1-year forward covering year $t$. No-arbitrage requires: $$(1+s_t)^t = (1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}\,(1+f_{[t-1,t]})$$ so the forward is $$f_{[t-1,t]} = \frac{(1+s_t)^t}{(1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}} - 1$$ A cash flow at time $t$ is priced with its own spot: $PV = \frac{CF_t}{(1+s_t)^t}$.

widget.caption: Drag the spot rates $s_1,\dots,s_4$ and watch the implied 1-year forward rates update via $(1+s_t)^t=(1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}(1+f)$. An upward-sloping spot curve forces forwards *above* the spots; an inverted curve pushes them below — the forwards always 'lever' the curve's slope.

sections.title: Forward rate from two spot rates
sections.body: The 1-year spot rate is 4% and the 2-year spot rate is 5%. Find the 1-year forward rate for year 2.
steps: Note the forward (6%) sits *above* both spots — the upward curve forces year 2's marginal rate higher than the average.

sections.title: A multi-year forward locked in today
sections.body: The 1-year spot is 4% and the 3-year spot is 6%. Find the *2-year* forward rate covering years 2 and 3 — the single annual rate you could lock in today to grow money from end of year 1 to end of year 3.
steps: Split the 3-year path: grow 1 year at $s_1$, then 2 years at the forward $f$. No-arbitrage: $(1+s_3)^3 = (1+s_1)(1+f)^2$.
Take the square root (it covers *two* years): $1+f = \sqrt{1.145208} = 1.070144$, so $f \approx 7.01\%$.
Cross-check: the forward 7.01% sits *above* the 3-year spot 6%, exactly as a rising curve demands — the marginal future rate must exceed the cumulative average.

sections.title: Forwards exaggerate the curve's slope
sections.body: A reliable intuition: when the spot curve **rises**, each forward rate lies *above* the spot for that maturity; when it **falls** (inverted), forwards lie *below*. The forward is the marginal rate for one specific future year, so it must overshoot the cumulative average that the spot represents. If your computed forward sits between two rising spots, you made an arithmetic error.

sections.title: Discount each cash flow at its own spot rate
sections.body: The biggest term-structure error is discounting *all* cash flows at a single yield. With a term structure, a payment at time $t$ must be discounted at the **$t$-year spot rate** $s_t$, not at $s_1$ or some flat average. Mixing maturities under one rate misprices the bond. Second trap: forward-rate exponents — the $(t-1)$ and $t$ powers must match the spot maturities exactly, or the geometric link breaks.

cards.front: Why must a forward rate equal $\frac{(1+s_t)^t}{(1+s_{t-1})^{t-1}}-1$ rather than something you choose?
cards.back: Because two paths to the same maturity must accumulate identically or a riskless profit exists. Growing $t$ years at $s_t$ has to match growing $(t-1)$ years at $s_{t-1}$ then one year at the forward — solving that equality *forces* the forward; it is not a market quote you can set freely.

cards.front: On a rising spot curve, why does every forward sit above the spot for its maturity?
cards.back: The spot is the cumulative *average* rate to that point; the forward is the *marginal* rate for one specific later year. To pull a rising average upward, each new year's marginal rate must overshoot it — so forwards exaggerate the curve's slope.

questions.q: 1-year spot $=3\%$, 2-year spot $=4\%$. Find the 1-year forward rate for year 2.
Under a term structure, a \$1000 cash flow at year 3 with $s_3 = 6\%$ has present value:
questions.explain: Discount at its own 3-year spot rate: $1000/(1.06)^3$.

questions.q: If the spot curve is downward-sloping (inverted), the 1-year forward rates are generally:
questions.explain: A falling curve pushes the marginal forward rates below the spot rates.

questions.q: 2-year spot $=5\%$, and the 1-year forward for year 2 is $7\%$. Find the 1-year spot rate.
The forward rate $f_{[t-1,t]}$ represents:
choices: A future 1-year rate locked in today
questions.explain: It is the rate for the single future year $t$, implied (locked in) by today's spot curve.

concepts.title: Interest Rate Swaps
concepts.tagline: Trade a floating-rate obligation for a fixed one. The swap rate is the level fixed rate with the same present value as the expected floating payments.

sections.body: A company with a floating-rate loan hates uncertainty; another with a fixed loan wants to bet on falling rates. An **interest rate swap** lets them trade payment streams: one pays fixed, receives floating; the other does the reverse. No principal changes hands — only the interest difference. The exam asks you to find the fair **swap rate** and value an existing swap, both of which reduce to the spot curve you already know.

sections.title: A swap is a portfolio of forward rate agreements
sections.body: Each period of a swap exchanges a fixed payment for that period's floating rate — which, priced today, is the **forward rate**. So a swap is really a bundle of forward-rate agreements stacked across the term. The fair fixed rate (the **swap rate**) is the single level rate whose payments have the *same present value* as the whole strip of forward (floating) payments. Set the two legs' PVs equal and solve for the fixed rate.

sections.title: The swap rate
sections.body: Using spot rates $s_t$ and discount factors $P(0,t) = (1+s_t)^{-t}$, the level swap rate $R$ on notional 1 for $n$ years satisfies (fixed leg PV = floating leg PV): $$R = \frac{1 - P(0,n)}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} P(0,t)} = \frac{1 - (1+s_n)^{-n}}{\sum_{t=1}^n (1+s_t)^{-t}}$$ The numerator is the floating leg's value; the denominator is the annuity of discount factors.

sections.title: A two-year swap rate
sections.body: Spot rates are $s_1 = 4\%$ and $s_2 = 5\%$. Find the fixed swap rate on a 2-year swap.
steps: Floating leg value (numerator): $1 - P(0,2) = 1 - 0.90703 = 0.09297$.
Annuity of discount factors (denominator): $0.96154 + 0.90703 = 1.86857$.
$R = 0.09297 / 1.86857 = 0.04975 \approx 4.98\%$ — sensibly between the 1- and 2-year spots.

sections.title: What actually changes hands each period
sections.body: A company is the *fixed payer* on a swap with notional \$10 million and the fixed rate locked at 4.98% from the example above. For the coming year the floating reference rate sets at 6%. What is the net settlement, and who pays whom?
steps: The fixed payer owes fixed and is owed floating. Fixed leg this period $= 4.98\% \times 10{,}000{,}000 = \$498{,}000$.
Floating leg this period $= 6\% \times 10{,}000{,}000 = \$600{,}000$.
Net the two — **principal never moves**: the fixed payer receives $600{,}000 - 498{,}000 = \$102{,}000$.
Direction check: floating (6%) came in above the locked fixed (4.98%), so the fixed payer — who bet rates would rise — wins this period and collects the difference.

sections.title: Swap rate is a discount-factor-weighted average of forwards
sections.body: The swap rate always lands *between* the spot/forward rates across the term — it is essentially their present-value-weighted average. So a quick sanity check: a 2-year swap rate must sit between $s_1$ and $s_2$. If your answer falls outside that range, you inverted a discount factor. The numerator $1 - P(0,n)$ is also exactly the value of receiving all the floating payments — memorize that shortcut.

sections.title: Notional is not exchanged; net the payments
sections.body: Two recurring traps: (1) the **notional principal never changes hands** — only the *difference* between fixed and floating interest is settled each period, so don't add principal to either leg's cash flows. (2) To **value** an existing swap mid-life (not just find its initial rate), recompute both legs at the *current* spot curve; a swap is worth zero only at inception, then drifts as rates move.

cards.front: Why does the swap rate equal $\frac{1-P(0,n)}{\sum P(0,t)}$ instead of just averaging the spot rates?
cards.back: Because the fair fixed rate is the level rate whose discounted payments match the floating leg. The floating leg is worth exactly $1-P(0,n)$ today, and a level rate paid over the term is worth that rate times the annuity of discount factors $\sum P(0,t)$ — set them equal and the rate falls out. It is a present-value match, so it weights each period by its discount factor, not equally.

cards.front: Why is a brand-new swap worth zero, yet worth something a year later?
cards.back: The swap rate is *chosen* at inception to make the two legs' present values equal — zero by construction. Once rates move, the locked fixed leg no longer matches the revalued floating leg at the new spot curve, so the swap drifts to a positive value for one side and negative for the other.

questions.q: In a plain vanilla interest rate swap, what is exchanged each period?
questions.explain: Only the difference between the fixed and floating interest on the notional is settled; principal is never exchanged.

questions.q: Discount factors are $P(0,1)=0.95$ and $P(0,2)=0.89$. Find the 2-year swap rate.
The value of a newly initiated (fair) interest rate swap is:
questions.explain: By construction the swap rate equates the two legs' present values, so the swap is worth zero at inception.

questions.q: A 3-year swap has spot rates 3%, 4%, 5%. The swap rate must lie:
questions.explain: The swap rate is a discount-factor-weighted average of the term structure, so it falls within the spot range.

questions.q: To value an existing swap two years into its life, you should:
choices: Use the original swap rate's discount factors
Recompute both legs at the current spot curve
Assume it is still worth zero
Add the notional to the fixed leg
questions.explain: A swap is zero-value only at inception; afterward revalue both legs at the prevailing spot rates.

concepts.title: Duration & Immunization
concepts.tagline: Duration is how rate-sensitive a cash flow is. Immunization is matching that sensitivity so a rate move can't hurt you.

sections.body: When interest rates move, the value of every future cash flow moves with them. **Duration** measures exactly how much, and **immunization** is the art of arranging assets so that a rate shock leaves your surplus untouched. This is the conceptual peak of FM — and a favorite of the exam writers.

sections.title: Duration is the cash flow's center of gravity in time
sections.body: Picture each payment as a weight placed on a timeline, the weight being its present value. **Macaulay duration** is the balance point of those weights — the average time, PV-weighted, at which you get paid. Longer duration means cash arrives later, which means *more* sensitivity to rate changes. **Modified duration** then converts that into the percentage price drop per 1% rate rise.

sections.title: Duration and convexity
sections.body: Macaulay duration: $$D_{mac} = \frac{\sum t\, v^t\, CF_t}{\sum v^t\, CF_t} = \frac{\sum t\,\cdot PV_t}{P}$$ Modified duration: $D_{mod} = \dfrac{D_{mac}}{1+i}$. First-order price change: $$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i$$ Convexity adds the second-order correction $+\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2$.

sections.title: Duration of a two-payment stream
sections.body: Cash flows of \$100 at year 1 and \$100 at year 2, at $i = 10\%$. Find the Macaulay duration.

sections.title: Building an immunized portfolio
sections.body: A liability of \$1000 (present value) comes due with duration 6 years. You can buy two assets: stream A with duration 4 and stream B with duration 9. How do you split \$1000 so a small rate move can't dent your surplus?
steps: Condition 1 — match present value: invest the full \$1000, so $PV_{assets} = PV_{liability}$ automatically.
Condition 2 — match duration: let $w$ be the fraction in A. Portfolio duration is the PV-weighted average $4w + 9(1-w)$, and we need it to equal the liability's 6.
Solve: $4w + 9 - 9w = 6 \Rightarrow 9 - 5w = 6 \Rightarrow w = 0.6$. So **\$600 in A and \$400 in B**.

Condition 3 — convexity: spreading the assets to durations 4 and 9 around the liability's 6 (a 'barbell') gives the asset side *more* spread in time than the single liability, so asset convexity exceeds liability convexity — Redington's third condition is met.
Cross-check: $0.6(4) + 0.4(9) = 2.4 + 3.6 = 6.0$ years. Durations match, so a small rate shock moves assets and liability by the same first-order amount — the surplus is protected.
sections.answer: \$600 in the 4-year asset, \$400 in the 9-year asset

sections.title: Estimate price moves with one multiplication
sections.body: Once you have modified duration, a rate change's price impact is a single product: $\Delta P/P \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i$. A bond with $D_{mod} = 7$ loses about 7% if rates rise 1%. This linear estimate is exam-fast; convexity only matters when they ask for a refined answer on a large rate move.

sections.title: Forgetting the Redington conditions
sections.body: Immunization is not just matching present values. **Redington immunization** needs three conditions: (1) asset PV = liability PV, (2) asset duration = liability duration, and (3) asset convexity > liability convexity. Skip the convexity condition and your 'immunized' portfolio still loses to large rate moves. All three must hold.

cards.front: Why does longer duration mean a bond is more rate-sensitive?
cards.back: Duration is the PV-weighted average time you wait to be paid. Cash that arrives later is discounted by a higher power of $v$, so a change in the rate compounds over more periods — its present value swings more. A long-duration bond has its weight far out in time, so the same rate move hits it harder: $\Delta P/P \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i$.

cards.front: Why isn't matching present values enough to immunize — what do the duration and convexity conditions add?
cards.back: Equal PVs only protect against *no* rate change. Matching duration makes assets and liabilities move by the same *first-order* amount when rates shift, so the surplus stays flat to first order. Requiring asset convexity to exceed liability convexity makes the second-order term work in your favor, so the surplus can only improve — never fall — for any small move in either direction.

questions.q: A zero-coupon bond pays \$1000 in 7 years. What is its Macaulay duration?
questions.explain: A single payment's PV-weighted average time is just its own maturity: 7 years. A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its time to maturity.

questions.q: A bond has modified duration 6. If interest rates rise by 0.5%, the approximate percentage price change is:
questions.explain: $\Delta P/P \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i = -6(0.005) = -0.03 = -3\%$.

questions.q: If Macaulay duration is 8.4 years and $i = 5\%$, find the modified duration.
Which is NOT a required condition for Redington immunization?
choices: PV of assets equals PV of liabilities
Duration of assets equals duration of liabilities
Convexity of assets exceeds convexity of liabilities
Asset cash flows occur before liability cash flows
All three standard conditions hold simultaneously
questions.explain: Redington requires equal PVs, equal durations, and greater asset convexity. There is no requirement that asset cash flows precede liabilities — that describes exact (dedicated) matching, not Redington immunization.

questions.q: Two equal-PV cash flow streams have durations 4 and 9 years. To immunize a liability of duration 6 using both, the weight on the 4-year stream is closest to:
questions.explain: Solve $4w + 9(1-w) = 6 \Rightarrow 9 - 5w = 6 \Rightarrow 5w = 3 \Rightarrow w = 0.6 = 60\%$.

concepts.title: Convexity & Cash-Flow Matching
concepts.tagline: Duration is the straight-line estimate; convexity is the curve it misses. Exact matching sidesteps both by funding each liability directly.

sections.body: Duration assumes the price-rate relationship is a straight line — but it is actually a **curve**, bowed toward the origin. **Convexity** measures that curvature, and it is always your friend: it makes bonds gain a little more when rates fall and lose a little less when they rise. The exam tests convexity as a second-order correction and contrasts immunization with its airtight cousin, **exact cash-flow matching**.

sections.title: The price curve bows above the duration line
sections.body: Plot bond price against interest rate: it slopes down (higher rates, lower price) but **curves upward** — convex. Duration is the tangent line at today's rate, a decent estimate for small moves but it underestimates the price for *any* move, up or down, because the true curve lies above the tangent. Convexity quantifies that gap. More convexity means more cushion against large rate swings — a desirable, free-ish property.

sections.title: Second-order price change and matching
sections.body: The Taylor expansion of price in the rate adds a convexity term: $$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D_{mod}\,\Delta i + \tfrac{1}{2}\,C\,(\Delta i)^2$$ where convexity $C = \frac{1}{P}\frac{d^2P}{di^2} = \frac{\sum t(t+1)\,v^{t+2} CF_t}{P}$ (one common form). **Exact (dedicated) matching:** choose assets whose cash flows *equal* each liability at every date — then no rate move matters at all, no duration or convexity needed.

sections.title: Convexity-adjusted price change
sections.body: A bond has modified duration 8 and convexity 120. Rates rise by 2% ($\Delta i = 0.02$). Estimate the percentage price change with and without the convexity correction.
steps: Adjusted estimate: $-16\% + 2.4\% = -13.6\%$.
Convexity softens the loss — the true drop is smaller than duration alone predicts.

sections.title: Dedicating assets to liabilities (exact matching)
sections.body: You owe \$1000 at the end of year 1 and \$1000 at the end of year 2. Two assets are available: a 1-year zero (pays its face at year 1) and a 2-year bond with a 5% annual coupon (pays 5% of face at year 1 and 105% at year 2). Find the face amounts that fund the liabilities *exactly*, with no rate risk.
steps: Always work from the **last** liability backward, because only the long bond reaches year 2. Let $F_B$ be the face of the 2-year bond. Its year-2 payment is $1.05\,F_B$, which must equal \$1000: $F_B = 1000/1.05 = \$952.38$.
That bond also throws off a year-1 coupon: $0.05 \times 952.38 = \$47.62$.
The remaining year-1 need is $1000 - 47.62 = \$952.38$, funded by the 1-year zero: buy face $F_A = \$952.38$.

Cross-check year 1: $952.38$ (zero) $+ 47.62$ (coupon) $= \$1000$. Year 2: $1.05(952.38) = \$1000$. Both dates land exactly — and because each cash flow is matched at its own date, **no rate move can ever create a shortfall**, and nothing needs rebalancing.

sections.title: Convexity always helps the holder
sections.body: The convexity term is $+\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2$ — and since $(\Delta i)^2 \ge 0$ and $C > 0$ for ordinary bonds, it is **always positive**, whether rates rise or fall. So for two bonds with equal duration, the more convex one is strictly preferable: it falls less and rises more. This is exactly why Redington immunization demands asset convexity *greater* than liability convexity — the surplus stays non-negative for moves in either direction.

sections.title: Matching vs immunization are different guarantees
sections.body: Don't conflate the two strategies. **Exact matching** funds each liability with an asset cash flow of the same amount and date — perfect protection, but often impractical or expensive. **Immunization** (Redington) only matches PV, duration, and convexity, protecting against *small* parallel rate shifts; it can still fail under large or non-parallel moves. Matching needs no rebalancing; immunization must be **rebalanced** as time passes and rates move, since durations drift.

cards.front: Why does positive convexity help the holder whether rates rise OR fall?
cards.back: The correction term is $+\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2$. Since $(\Delta i)^2$ is positive for any non-zero move and $C>0$ for ordinary bonds, the term is always positive. So the true price beats the duration line in both directions — bigger gain when rates fall, smaller loss when they rise. That free cushion is why two equal-duration bonds aren't equal: pick the more convex one.

cards.front: Exact matching needs no rebalancing but immunization does — why the difference?
cards.back: Exact (dedicated) matching funds each liability with a cash flow of the same amount on the same date, so the match is locked in regardless of rates and time. Immunization only matches PV, duration and convexity *today*; as time passes and rates move, durations drift apart and the match degrades — so it must be periodically rebalanced to stay protective.

questions.q: A bond has modified duration 5 and convexity 80. For $\Delta i = +0.01$, the convexity correction to $\Delta P/P$ is:
The convexity adjustment to a bond's price change is:
questions.explain: $\tfrac12 C(\Delta i)^2 \ge 0$ for ordinary bonds regardless of the direction of the rate move.

questions.q: Two bonds have equal duration. The one with higher convexity will:
choices: Outperform for large rate moves either way
questions.explain: Greater convexity means it falls less and rises more, so it outperforms when rates move substantially in either direction.

questions.q: Which strategy provides protection without any need to rebalance over time?
questions.explain: Exact (dedicated) matching funds each liability directly, so it needs no rebalancing and is immune to any rate change.

questions.q: Compared to the duration-only estimate, including positive convexity makes the predicted price for a rate increase:
questions.explain: The positive convexity term offsets part of the duration loss, raising the predicted price (a smaller drop).

concepts.title: Determinants of Interest Rates
concepts.tagline: Where rates come from: a real return, an inflation premium, and compensation for default, liquidity, and maturity risk. The qualitative capstone.

sections.body: Every rate you have discounted with on this exam is built from parts. A lender demands a **real** return for deferring consumption, plus compensation for **inflation**, plus premiums for the chance of **default**, for tying money up (**liquidity**), and for the **term** of the loan. Understanding this decomposition is the qualitative capstone of FM — and the SOA tests it directly.

sections.title: Stack the compensations a lender requires
sections.body: Start with the **real risk-free rate** — what you'd earn with no inflation and no risk, purely for waiting. Add an **inflation premium** so your repayment keeps its purchasing power. Then layer risk premiums: a **default (credit)** premium for the borrower possibly not paying, a **liquidity** premium if the asset is hard to sell, and a **maturity/term** premium for longer commitments. The quoted nominal rate is the sum of all these demands.

sections.title: Fisher equation and the rate stack
sections.body: The **Fisher equation** links nominal $i$, real $r$, and inflation $\pi$: $$(1+i) = (1+r)(1+\pi) \;\approx\; i \approx r + \pi$$ The full nominal rate is approximately $$i \approx r + \pi + (\text{default}) + (\text{liquidity}) + (\text{maturity premium})$$ Real rate exactly: $1 + r = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}$.

sections.title: Real rate via the Fisher equation
sections.body: A bond yields a nominal 8% while inflation runs 3%. Find the exact real rate of return.
steps: Fisher (exact): $1 + r = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi} = \frac{1.08}{1.03}$.
The quick approximation $r \approx i - \pi = 8\% - 3\% = 5\%$ is close but slightly overstates it.
The gap (5% vs 4.85%) is the cross-term $r\pi$ the approximation drops.

sections.title: Building a quoted rate from its parts
sections.body: A lender prices a loan to a moderately risky, somewhat illiquid borrower. The real risk-free rate is 2%, expected inflation is 3%, the default premium is 1.5%, and the liquidity premium is 0.5%. What nominal rate should they quote?
steps: Combine the real rate and inflation exactly via Fisher: $(1.02)(1.03) = 1.0506$, a risk-free nominal of $\approx 5.06\%$.
Stack the risk premiums on top: default $1.5\%$ + liquidity $0.5\% = 2.0\%$.
Quoted nominal $\approx 5.06\% + 2.0\% = 7.06\%$.

Cross-check with the fast additive form: $2 + 3 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 7.0\%$ — within a few basis points, the gap being the dropped $r\pi$ cross-term. Each piece is a distinct demand the lender makes; strip one away (say the loan becomes risk-free) and the quote drops by exactly that premium.

sections.title: Approximate, then refine with Fisher
sections.body: For a fast estimate use $r \approx i - \pi$; it is within a few basis points for ordinary rates. When precision matters, switch to the exact $1+r = \frac{1+i}{1+\pi}$, which always gives a *slightly lower* real rate than the subtraction (the dropped $r\pi$ term is positive). Knowing the direction of the error lets you sanity-check multiple-choice answers instantly.

sections.title: Real vs nominal, and which premium is which
sections.body: Keep the layers straight: a **higher inflation** expectation raises the *nominal* rate but not the real rate; a **riskier borrower** raises the *default* premium; an illiquid asset raises the *liquidity* premium. Confusing inflation compensation with a risk premium is the classic conceptual slip. And don't subtract inflation twice — the nominal rate already includes it, so the *real* return is what's left after removing it once.

cards.front: Why does the exact real rate always come out a touch below the $i-\pi$ approximation?
cards.back: Fisher says $(1+i)=(1+r)(1+\pi)=1+r+\pi+r\pi$. The quick subtraction $r\approx i-\pi$ throws away the positive cross-term $r\pi$, so it overstates the real rate slightly. Solving exactly, $1+r=\frac{1+i}{1+\pi}$, restores that term and lands just under the approximation — handy for ruling out the too-high multiple-choice answer.

cards.front: Why does higher expected inflation raise the nominal rate but leave the real rate roughly unchanged?
cards.back: Inflation compensation is a *separate layer* in the rate stack from the real return. Lenders add a bigger inflation premium so repayment keeps its purchasing power — that lifts the quoted nominal rate — but the real reward for waiting (and the default/liquidity premiums) is unaffected. Mixing up the inflation layer with a risk premium is the classic conceptual slip.

questions.q: Nominal rate 10%, inflation 4%. Find the exact real rate.
questions.explain: $1+r = 1.10/1.04 = 1.05769$, so $r \approx 5.77\%$ — just under the $6\%$ approximation.

questions.q: Which premium compensates a lender for the risk that the borrower may not repay?
questions.explain: The default or credit risk premium covers the chance of non-repayment.

questions.q: By the Fisher equation, the approximation $i \approx r + \pi$ omits which term?
questions.explain: $(1+r)(1+\pi) = 1 + r + \pi + r\pi$; the approximation drops the cross-term $r\pi$.

questions.q: All else equal, an increase in expected inflation primarily raises the:
questions.explain: Inflation expectations are passed into the nominal rate, leaving the real rate roughly unchanged.

questions.q: An asset that is difficult to sell quickly without a price concession commands a higher:
questions.explain: Hard-to-trade assets carry a liquidity premium to compensate holders for that difficulty.
